items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Following discussions in the
Business Committee yesterday, I seek leave for Wednesday, 14 November 2012 to be a
members’ day, despite Standing Order 74(1), and for any bills drawn from the ballot on
Thursday, 8 November to be set down fo r first reading on Wednesday, 14 November,
despite Standing Order 281(2).

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is none.
Economy and Government Financial Position—Reports
1. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What reports has he
received on the Government’s financial position?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Crown’s financial statements for
the 3 months to 30 September were issued t oday. They confirm that the Government is
keeping its spending under cont rol, but that revenue can be  affected by the uncertain
global economic situation and its impact on New Zealand. For example, in the first 3
months of this fiscal year Crown tax re venue was $295 million below forecast and core
Crown interest revenue was $147 million lower than expected. This was partially offset
by Crown expenses being $200 million below fo recast, including slightly lower than
forecast welfare expenses. The operating deficit before gains and losses was $2 billion
for the 3-month period.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What approach is the Government taking to ensure it continues to
carefully manage its finances so it does return to surplus?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government’s target is to return to surplus by 2014-15
so that we will then have choices about repaying debt, resuming contributions to the
New Zealand Superannuation Fund, or targe ting more investment in priority public
services. To achieve this we will need to keep on top of the factors we can control, such
as remaining prudent with any new spending and borrowing. We will also continue to
focus very strongly on delivering more public services, even where there is less money,
to ensure that we s upport those who need ou r services. This is important in a world
where economic conditions are unpredictable and could have unpredictable impacts on
New Zealand Government revenue.

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: What reports has he received  on the global ec onomic situation
and its likely impact on New Zealand and Government finances?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Earlier this week Treas ury published its monthly Economic
Indicators for November, focusing on global growt h. It notes that more than 5 years
after the onset of the financial crisis th e world economy is performing again below
expectation. World economic growth in the first half of 2012 wa s generally below IMF
forecasts, and the latest forecast for world out put, issued last month, contained further
downward revisions. If global growth does remain weaker than expected, it would affect
New Zealand’s growth and Government finances.
6346 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2012

items.speaker: Hon Tau Henare
items.text: How is New Zealand’s economy performing compared with most
other developed economies, and what policy pr escription would put this performance at
risk?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: We continue to perform at m oderate levels, but nevertheless
better than most other develope d countries. In the first half  of this year New Zealand
grew by 1.6 percent, which is higher than growth rates in the US, Japan, Canada, the
UK, and the euro area over the same period. Our quarterly growth rate is about the same
as Australia’s. Policies that would put th is at risk would include borrowing more,
spending more, and printing money, which would fuel costs for households and
businesses and put jobs at risk.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can the Minister stand in this House and pretend that it is
good news that the Government deficit of $2.1 billion is $490 million—or 27 percent—
higher than he projected in his Budget just months ago?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am not saying it is good news; I am just saying it is the
news. It is the news and it is  a snapshot in a long journey towards repairing the damage
that the previous Labour Government did to the economy and to Government finances.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is it correct that in addition to an increasing Government deficit,
the New Zealand economy is running the se cond-worst current account deficit in the
developed world this year, and is projec ted by the IMF to have the worst current
account deficit in the developed world next ye ar; if it is correct, doe s he agree with the
Governor of the Reserve Bank, Mr Wheeler, that that is far too high?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: On the first issue, of course we want to see the Government
deficit coming back. It was $18 billion 2 y ears ago, it was $9 billion last year, and we
are on the track towards about $7 billion for this year and a $2 billion deficit the
following year. Quarterly figures  are not pushing us off that  track. In respect of the
current account deficit, I would take more no tice of what the member said if it had not
been the case that under his Government it doubled from 4 percent to 8 percent, which
were the worst levels New Zealand has ever had. That was from the party that is now
preaching the loudest about fixing it.
Schools, Canterbury—Proposed Closures and Mergers and Confidence in Minister
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in all his Ministers; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes; because they are working harder for a
brighter future for all New Zealanders.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he have confidence in hi s Minister of Education and her
management of the future of education in Christchurch; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes; because she is committing $1 billion to new schooling in
Christchurch. I think what we all need to understand in respect  of Christchurch is that a
major earthquake took place that has changed the patterns of where people live. But it
has also presented an opportunity to deliver 21 st century schools to Christchurch. I
simply make this point: we are not rebu ilding the central business district in
Christchurch with exactly the same buildi ngs; we are using the opportunity to deliver
arguably the most liveable city in New Zeal and, and then maybe, just maybe, there will
be an opportunity to deliver better schooling facilities for yo ungsters in Christchurch. I
think that is a good thing.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his undertaki ng that he will personally look
through the response from each Christchurch school; if so, why does he think it is
necessary for a Prime Minister to personally review submissions from all these schools
if he does in fact have confidence in his Minister?
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6347

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, and I would point out that  the Minister is personally
visiting all of the schools. I understand that 35 of the 37 schools have  agreed to that.
Why am I personally doing that? Well, I take a personal interest in Christchurch. It is
one of the Government’s four key priorities , and I gave that commitment to the people
of Christchurch because they kept on read ing nonsense from Chris Hipkins that was
getting printed in the Press.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why will his Government not tell the communities affected by the
closure and merger proposals what all the options identified by the ministry are?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The purpose now is, with those affected schools, to go through
all of the options for those clusters, to ta lk about what the optio ns might be and the
reasons why, and to potenti ally come up with some good solutions. What the
Government is saying to the people of Christ church, to those parents who are affected,
and to those schools, is that  we are listening to you, but we  are also listening to the
advice we are receiving about what is changi ng. We are going to spend a billion dollars
over the next 10 years—

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I have been listening for quite a
while. I actually asked why he will not tell us what the options are that were put forward
by the Ministry of Education.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member is welcome to repeat his question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Why will his Government not tell the communities affected by
closure and merger proposals what all the options identified by the ministry are?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have all of that detail  to hand. I know what is being
proposed there. So you might do best to ask th at question of the Minister herself. But
the point is we are now engaging in a full communication process with those schools.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The question was not what
those options were. It was w hy the Minister would not tell us what those options were.
The Minister has not addressed the question at all.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the Prime Minister has, in  that he said he cannot tell the
House what those options are because he doe s not have them. That  kind of detail, he
recommended, should be directed to the Mi nister of Education, and that is not
unreasonable.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. No one was asking the
Prime Minister what the options were. Th e question was why his Minister is not
releasing those options. Sh e is the person who has refused, under the Official
Information Act—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is getting into debate on the matter. The Prime
Minister welcomed members to question the Minister of Education on the matter, and
that is not an unreasonable response from the Prime Minister. The member asked why
he is not releasing that information. The Prime Minister said to address that to the
Minister. He has obviously made it clear th at there is no Government policy not to
release that information.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Will he instruct the Ministry of Education, through his Minister, to
release the ministry’s advice on the future of Christchurch education, which my office
requested under the Official Information Ac t, and which has been withheld by the
ministry on the basis that there “does not  appear to be overriding public-interest
reasons” to support the release?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, because I think the primary objective at the moment is to
engage in good consultation with those schools and clusters, and that is what the
Government is doing.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Spea ker. That question was really about
whether he will instruct the ministry.
6348 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2012

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In fairness, the Prime Minister did say that, no, he would not.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Is it acceptable that the schools proposed to be closed or merged
have not been advised as to whether they will be allowed additional time to respond to
the proposals, even though they have not yet received all the relevant information from
the ministry?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I may stand to be corrected, but  my understanding is that the
Minister is talking to  the schools about giving them additional time in working their
way through the process. I may be wrong, but that was the last c onversation I had with
her.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: When did the Minister first make  him aware of the data areas,
including data on roll numbers, number of buildings, presence of facilities, and damage,
that were included in the docum ents issued to schools as pa rt of the rationale for the
proposals?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I was aware after the schools had the information and had
identified that they were in the list of school s that could be either merged or closed, or
whatever it might be, that there was some discrepancy between the schools’ data and the
ministry’s. A lot of data is agreed and corr ect, and some is not. Some of it is for very
technical reasons in the way that they part icularly count things. Some of it has been
subsequently updated, because there was a gap in one particular period. But, again, all
of that is largely an irrele vance, because in th e end the schools, th e clusters, and the
Government are going to sit down on an agreed plan. They may disagree over time, they
may choose to disagree, but the data will be agreed before we go forward.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am sorry, Mr Speaker, but
it was a “when” question. I understand that th e Minister went through and listed them.
The question was when did he find out. We did not hear when. We heard a long list.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have already invited the Leader of the Opposition to repeat one
question. I believe that the question was a little longer than that. I cannot remember now
the detail of the question, and the Prime Mini ster, I believe, responded. His answer was
reasonable.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I think I made it quite clear. I said that sometime after the data
had been released, I was aware that there was a discrepancy betw een what the schools
thought and what the ministry thought. That was the time when I was aware. Rusty,
open up your ears, son.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] No, order! I must ask the Prime Minister to
withdraw that last statement. That is not acceptable.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I withdraw.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Under a point of order, that to me is not acceptable.
Canterbury, Recovery—Skills for Canterbury Programme Funding
3. COLIN KING (National—Kaik ōura) to the Minister for Tertiary Education,

items.speaker: Skills and Employment
items.text: How is the Government helpin g Cantabrians upskill for the
Christchurch rebuild?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for T ertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): Last week the Government announced that it has committed a further
$28 million from the Skills for Canterbury c ontingency to maintain the extended
training pipeline for tradespeople for the Ca nterbury rebuild. This ensures that in 2013
providers will be able to bu ild on the additional 3,500 trade training places and student
support provided over the last 2 years. Christ church will require t housands of builders,
plumbers, landscapers, electricians, and engi neers. It is crucial we have sufficient
skilled tradespeople to meet this demand. The trade training funding under Skills for
Canterbury is helping to ensure sufficient appropriately skilled people will be available.
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6349

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: How much has been invested to date in the Skills for Canterbury
initiative?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The amount spent in total to date is now $65.2 million. This
includes $16.7 million from Tertiary Educati on Commission baselines, $11.7 million of
reprioritisation from polytechs and institutes of technology, and now $36.8 million from
the Skills for Canterbury contingency. This money is invested in places this year and
last year, with similar numbers to be available in 2013. Initiatives include the Pacific
trades initiative, the M āori Trade Training initiativ e, and funding for the new
Canterbury Skills and Employment  Hub. Can I say that there are places available right
now for people to be involved in the Christchurch rebuil d. The Stronger Christchurch
Infrastructure Rebuild Team, for example, is recruiting for around a thousand people to
be trained and employed for the rebuild, and I strongly encourage anyone who is
interested in being part of it to contact their local training provider and find out the
opportunities available to them.

items.speaker: Colin King
items.text: Has he seen any other proposals about how the Government might have
allocated the funding?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Indeed, I have seen and received a number of suggestions
over the last year advocating that the entire Skills for Canterbury contingency fund be
spent immediately, if not sooner, irrespective  of need, rather than  on an as-required
basis. These proposals came from a group of people whose definition of success is
entirely about how much money they can s hove out the door as quickly as possible,
rather than what is required. These people have no concept of how to balance the books.
I am, of course, referring to the New Zealand Labour Party.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The Minister was lucky that was the very last word he said.
He should not attribute his summary of policies to another party, especially in response
to a question from his own colleague.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Was he advised in March this year that in order to meet the
demands of the rebuild ther e was a requirement for a th ousand additional Stronger
Christchurch Infrastructure Rebuild Team pl aces to be established in 2012; if so, why
was there an 8-month delay before Minister Brownlee launched the team’s training and
employment programme on 1 November 2012?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: In response to the question, of course it was required—it
was needed in 2012 and it has been provided in 2012.

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: I seek leave to table a document, a briefing from the Tertiary
Education Commission to Minister Joyce dated 28 March, which shows a requirement
for a thousand additional places made in 2012, made up of 500—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Leave is sought to tabl e that document. Is there any
objection? There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
Unemployment—September 2012 Quarterly Employment Survey and Comparison
of Forecasts
4. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance : In Budget 2011
which year was unemployment forecast to fall  below 5 percent and when does Treasury
now predict unemployment to fall below 5 percent?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In Budget 2011 Treasury predicted
unemployment would fall below 5 percent in the 2012-13 year. Right now it is updating
its forecast for the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, which will be released in
December. I would expect that it would be some years later that unemployment will fall
below 5 percent.
6350 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2012

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. That question was on
notice, and it did not ask what Treasury’s fu ture projections were. It asked what its
current projection is—when it predicts unemployment to fall below 5 percent.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the Minister has that information, that would be helpful.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am just checking the inform ation further in the Budget. If
by “now” the member means Budget 2012, which is the most recent Treasury
projection, back in May, it forecast unemplo yment would go below 5 percent in 2015-

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he stand by his election promise to create 170,000 more
jobs by 2015; if so, how many extra jobs have been created since that promise was
made?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It was a forecast, not a promise, because, unlike the Labour
Party, the Government does not actually create jobs directly. In fact, Government jobs
are shrinking. Government jobs are shrinking. It is businesses that create jobs, and there
have been tens of thousands of new jobs. There are more New Zealanders than ever in a
job today.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: According to the quarterly em ployment survey, did the number
of filled full-time jobs increase or decrease in the September quarter?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the quarterly employme nt survey had the number of
full-time jobs decreasing and the number of  part-time jobs increasing. Part of the
increase in those part-time jobs is likely to include people who are re sponding to the
Government’s clear signals about changes in welfare policy, and therefore are taking up
part-time work where they were not before. We regard that as success. Of course we
would like to see more full-time jobs, but in the last quarter there were not more full-
time jobs.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: According to yesterday’s quart erly employment survey, are
there more jobs or fewer jobs in the manufacturing industry than there were a year ago?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I think the survey shows there are fewer jobs in the
manufacturing industry, but they  still have not been able to  manufacture a crisis in the
way that the Opposition is trying to. The fact is that we have grumpy growth. We are
going to grow between 2 and 3 percent pret ty consistently. Some sectors and some
businesses are losing jobs; some sectors and some businesses are flat out trying to
recruit people—in fact, they ca nnot get the skills that they need. We would expect that
this will be the pattern for the foreseeable future.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: In the history of the quarterly employment survey data series,
which goes back to 1989, has there ever been a quarter with fewer filled jobs in
manufacturing than the September 2012 quarter?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do not know the answer to  that, but I would warn the
member that you cannot run economic policy o ff quarterly surveys, particularly when
quarterly figures are so volatile.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table a document from the Parliamentary Library
showing the number of filled jobs in the manufacturing sector is the lowest recorded
since the data series began in 1989.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6351
Tax Credits—Access to In-work Tax Credit
5. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister of Revenue : How
many parents have lost access to the in-work ta x credit in the past year because they
have lost their jobs or no longer work enough hours to qualify?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The member should not be surprised
that my answer is exactly the same as I gave to her written question No. 8951 barely 3
weeks ago—namely, the Inland Revenue Department does not specifically record why a
recipient does not receive a particular co mponent of Working for Families tax credits.
Entitlement to each component can start and stop throughout the year, depending on the
family circumstances, all of which cannot be accurately separated or identified to
answer this question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is the Minister content to allow this financial support to be
taken away from children whose parents lose their jobs through no fault of their own?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: What the member overlooks is that there are a range of other
support mechanisms in place to help parents in  that situation, and as a consequence of
those other support mechanisms, the curren t practice, introduced by the previous
Government, with regard to the operation of the in-work tax credit is appropriate.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How can the Minister claim th at the current support for those
families who lose their jobs is adequate for children, when the family tax credits and
benefits combined still leave 70 percent of the children in those families in poverty, the
jobs do not exist for their parents, and we know that the in-work tax credit amount alone
can significantly relieve that poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: There are two reasons for my comment. The first is that the
OECD has made it very clear that in its judgment—and New Zealand is part of the
OECD and generally respects its judgments in these resp ects—child poverty is best
helped through workforce participation and encouraging workforce participation. The
second part of my answer is that the member is selective in terms of the benefits that she
makes reference to. In addition to those that she commented upon, families in that
situation would also be entitled to the unemployment benefit and they may be entitled to
sole parent support, an accommodation supp lement, an emergency benefit, various
training allowances, a child disa bility allowance or  disability allowa nce, and, possibly,
after-school allowances. So if  she wants to make the co mparison, she should put the
whole suite of measures on the table, and not just a selected number of them.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is the Minister aware that every 3 months 75,000 hard-working
people, including thousands of parents,  become unemployed under the Key-Dunne
Government, and how is it fair to take away  the in-work tax credit from them and their
children when they lose their jobs in those difficult times?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I have got no idea where the member draws her figure from.
I think it is a figment of her imagination. The point—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: From your own ministry.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The member says it is from my own ministry. In my original
answer I made it very clear that because of the nature of the way in which these
interactions occur it is impossible to iden tify the numbers involved. The member seems
to deny that. But the point that I was making in my original supplementary answer—and
I will make it again—is that the member is being very selective. She is drawing on a
range of issues only. There are a number of mechanisms available to help families in
that situation, and the member should put all of those on the table when considering this
question.
6352 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2012

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How is it fair that the childr en of 40,000 hard-working people who
lost manufacturing jobs in the last 4 years of the Key-Dunne Government should also be
financially punished by having their in-work tax credit taken away as well?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: My answer is the same as it has been to previous iterations
of this type of example. But I would make one other point: what the member’s
legislation proposes is creating a disincentive for low-income working families to
remain in employment. One of the whole reasons why the Working for Families in-
work tax credit was introduced in the first place was to actually make it more palatable
and more attractive for those low-income fa milies to be in employment. The member
wants to actually turn that on its head, and make more peopl e reliant on the system as
beneficiaries, rather than do what every ot her country does and seek  to encourage them
into paid employment.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: If the Minister is so worried about incentivising people who work,
why does he then deny the tax credit to up to 40 percent of sole parent beneficiaries who
are in part-time work, whose children are ve ry likely to suffer the worst effects of long-
term poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I should point out to the member that there are a number of
other tax credit mechanisms available to help families in the type of situation she refers
to—for instance, the family tax credit, the minimum family tax credit, and the parental
tax credit. When you add all of those things together—and they ar e regularly adjusted
for inflation—they provide a substantial uplif t for families in that situation. They also
ensure that low-income working families are recognised for their efforts and, as a
consequence, encouraged and incentivised to remain in employment.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was not about other
kinds of tax credits. It wa s an explicit question about working people who are denied
the in-work tax credit, and I do not believe that the Minister answered that question
properly.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If I recollect correctly, the member started her question with “Given
the Minister’s such-and-such, how can it be fa ir …”, or “How does he believe it is fair
for something …”, and the Minister answered th at he believed it was fair because these
people have other things available to them.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Minister dismiss my compromise to him to extend the
in-work tax credit for 6 months to those w ho lose their jobs—a compromise that would
relieve some of the worst financial stress for children and for families at a very difficult
and insecure time when their parents lose their work?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: Two reasons: firstly, the point I made earlier about
employment and encouraging people into workforce participation, and, secondly—again
consistent with OECD stra tegy—employing policies that make work pay. What the
member’s bill does is create a disincentive for people at that low-income margin to be in
full-time employment. I think that is wrong.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister agree with economics professor Susan St John that
extending the in-work tax credit to all children below the current income threshold, even
if their parents are looking for work, ar e caring for grandchildren and receive
superannuation, or are studying, would be an  effective way to reduce poverty and
income inequality?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I seldom agree with Associate Professor St John.

items.text: Does the Minister agree with the statement from United Future
leader Peter Dunne when he pledged to Cl oser Together Whakatata Mai to “actively
support policy measures that reduce income in equality”; if so, why will he not support
my bill, which is just such a measure he pl edged to support, at least going to a select
committee?
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6353

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I do agree with that statement. The fact that as Minister of
Revenue over the last 7 years, under both Gove rnments, I have been part of seeing the
biggest shifts in personal tax rate reductions for the bottom two income steps is proof of
the point that I make.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: It’s not relieved poverty for the worst.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: The member says that does not  relieve poverty. What that
interjection proves is that this is a highly subjective rather than objective argument. My
focus has been on ensuring that our tax system  works fairly for those at the bottom of
the income scale. The last thing I want to see is a disincentive created for low-income
working people to remain in full-time employment, as the member’s bill would do.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why will not the Minister support this potential so lution at least
being considered by a select committee, wh en all the evidence suggests that it could
make the crucial difference to a quarter of a million Kiwi kids, and that he today could
be the difference between an empty and a full plate for many of these children?

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I reject that assertion entirely.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: You reject those children entirely.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: I am not rejecting those chil dren. That is a ridiculous
statement. What this is about is a good policy enviro nment that the previous
Government put in place called Working for Families. This Government is committed
to it. It ensures that low-income working peop le are rewarded for the fact that they are
in employment, consistent with internati onal standards. The best way to boost the
incomes of those households is through full-time employment, not through loading
them up on the beneficiary train, which the member wants to do.
Offenders, Rehabilitation—Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court Launch
6. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland)  to the Minister of Justice : How is the
Government reducing crime and reoffending by helping offenders to deal with their
addictions?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Last week I launched the new
alcohol and other drug courts in Auck land. This pilot programme will enable 100
offenders each year who are facing pris on sentences and who are prepared to
acknowledge their offending to participate in addiction tr eatment programmes, which
will be actively overseen by the courts. Similar programmes in other jurisdictions have
resulted in significant reductions in repeat offending. This Government is focused on
reducing crime in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: What else is the Government doing to reduce reoffending?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The justice sector has a target to reduce reoffending by
25 percent by 2017. The alcohol and other drug courts are part of a wider $10 million a
year package funded by alcohol  excise revenue and provid ing for early intervention
screening, a range of programmes for drink- drivers, youth alcohol and drug services,
and more training and development within workplaces. The Department of Corrections
has also invested heavily in drug and alcohol programmes in our prisons. This past year
we have seen a 6 percent drop in reoffending.
Hon Kate Wilkinson—Confidence

responsibilities, are not these the very areas where Kate W ilkinson was derelict in her
duty?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, I do not believe that accurately characterises it. I have
seen the letter that the honourable member wrote. I have also seen the response.
Looking at the response, it is quite clear that the Minister  took the correspondence very

the 2009 review. She spent some time looking at the operational capability. She also
indicated that the Department of Labour had said that there was no recent change in the
pattern of mining serious-harm  notifications that may give cause for concern. She has
acted pretty much on all of the advice that  I can see from the ministry, with the one
exception being where it did make a recommendation in relation to small mines, but the
reason she declined that is that, as the ministry itself said: “There are currently no mines
operating with fewer than 20 employees and existing operators already have systems, so
the above proposal would have no impact on any current mine operators.”
Hon Damien O’Connor: Given the rejection of advice on mine safety matters from
the unions, from her department’s internal review in 2008, and from my letter, how can
he be satisfied that this Mini ster has the level of judgment required to be a Minister in
his Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, if we want to get into the blame game, let us just start
having a look at a few of the facts. For a start-off, Labour was elected in 1999—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A question was asked, and a question as to the Prime
Minister’s confidence in Ministers is a fa ir question. I think it would be proper to
answer it and not to get into the blame game.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Let me reverse the order, then . In relation to the advice that
the Minister had, she received advice off the report that Tr evor Mallard had received in
2008. She followed that advice. In the advice, the Department of Labour said there were

sound. The operational capability of the mines inspectorate was sufficient.”, and I might
add that this was the advice that the Minister acted on. By the way, this was on the back
of the report that had been  received by Trevor Mallard wh en he was the Minister in

items.text: I think all of this Parliame nt would acknowledge that no

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON (Ministe r for Building and Construction)  on

families; if not, what other policy options is his Government considering?

items.text: That is an indicati on of a member who has

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Before he went on that trip, did the Attorney-General discuss with
him his recent trip to an Attorneys-Genera l conference in Australia, a conference that
focused on cyber-crime, and where the At torney-General spoke specifically on
extradition?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am very saddened to say this : no, he did not. It would have
been a fascinating trip, and I love my engagements with Chri s as he talks to me about
his international travels. I wish he had done it, because I would have listened very
carefully.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: Did the then commerce and justice Minister, Simon Power, discuss
intellectual property issues and his meeting with the Asia-Pacific head of the Motion
Picture Association of America, Mike Ellis, with him before or after he went on his US
trip?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No, and at the risk of offendi ng a colleague who has now left,
can I say also that I thoroughl y enjoyed my conversations I had with Simon Power on a
range of issues, but this was not one of them.
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6361
Television, Switch-over to Digital—TV TakeBack Programme
12. CHRIS AUCHINVOLE (National)  to the Minister for the Environment :
How many televisions have been collected  to date under the Government’s TV
Takeback programme?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: In just over 1 month, 18,145
televisions have so far been  dropped off for recycling in  the Hawke’s Bay and on the
West Coast, which, as the first regions to ma ke the switch to digi tal television, are the
first to be involved in th e Government’s TV TakeBack Programme. Based on the
average weight of a televisi on, this is the equivalent of  over 435 tonnes of waste
diverted from our landfills.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: What happens to the televisi ons once they are collected for
recycling?

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
items.text: Well, that is a good question. Televisions dropped off for
recycling are taken to national recycling facilities, where they are taken apart.
Components are recycled locally or sent overs eas to specialist recy cling facilities. The
material extracted has a variety of uses. Fo r example, glass from the screens can be
transformed into bunker sand for golf course s; copper around the electron gun can be
recycled into new cabling; and degaussing wire, which sits around the front of the
screen, is high-grade iron that can be re cycled into metal goods. Televisions also
contain materials that can be harmful if released into soil or waterways, such as lead,
mercury, and cadmium. Safe recycling takes away the risk of contamination and reduces
the volume of waste going into our landfills.
Question No. 10 to Minister

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I seek leave to table an answer to a
written question I have just received, which is  not publicly available, I believe. It shows
that the number of vacant State houses in New Zealand is 5 percent, unlike the answer
the Minister gave in the House just a few moments ago. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Leave has been sought, and there should be no interjection.
Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection? There is objection.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . That seeking of leave just brings to atte ntion the housing
problem that we have in New Zealand. When  you have 5 percent of our housing stock
currently not being used—tha t is around 3,300 homes that could actually house people
on lower incomes—that is a disgrace. That is a disgrace, because  right now people in
my electorate anyway are living in cars, in caravans, and two or three families to a
home, when they could actually be living in a State house instead.
There is a real problem in New Zealand with housing and housing affordability. No
longer is the Kiwi dream of owning your own home a real po ssibility for thousands and
thousands of Kiwis. No longer can you get a chance to be on that bottom rung of the
ladder. House prices have gone up in Auck land in particular, in Christchurch, in
Tauranga, and in a number of other places—in more than half of the country.
So it was with great anticipation, enormous anticipation, that we wanted to hear what
Bill English was going to announce to th e Productivity Commission’s report on
housing. We waited 7 months. We waited 7 months. The build-up was excruciating.
What did we get? An extraordinary le t-down—an extraordin ary let-down. They
weakened the Resource Management Act, they  lowered industry standards, they pushed
more responsibility on to councils, and they  tried to make land cheaper by expanding
the boundaries of Auckland, for example. So you have to get on to the motorway and
6362 General Debate 7 Nov 2012
drive for an hour, rather than actually do something intelligent, which is medium sized -
scale housing inside of Auckland.
That is it—that was it. That was to solv e New Zealand’s housi ng problem. It fails
utterly, and that is what everybody said—not ju st us, not just me and not just Annette
King, but, for example, the Mayor of Taura nga: “In my view it failed to take into
account the reality of the situation”, he sai d. Brian Fallow said: “It is fair to judge a
policy package like the one on housing affordab ility announced this week by what they
do to relieve those problems.”—those problems being housing affordability—“In short,
precious little.” John Armstrong wrote: “Pack age? What package? … The plan looks
like a rough first draft”. In other words, nobody is impresse d with this Government’s
performance on housing. It is woeful and it is disappointing.
There is a real shortage of houses for younge r people wanting to get that first chance
on the ladder, and this Government is determined not to do anything about it. It gives up
on the most basic things to do. One thing it might want to look at, for example, is a
capital gains tax, or at least not allow the price of houses to go through the roof, and at
least put our investment into productive en terprises rather than into the Auckland
property market.
Even when there is a possibility of St ate housing and community housing, as in the
Hobsonville scheme, the Government cancels it.  The Prime Minister calls it economic
vandalism—that is what he calls it, econom ic vandalism—to put social housing into a
housing development. Of the 3,000 houses, 1,000 were going to be houses that would
have been able to accommodate low-income families. The Government cut it from
1,000 to 100. And guess what? Now it is down to 17—17. And the Government
wonders why there is a housing affordability  problem! That is why there is a housing
affordability problem. It is because it is not doing anything about it.
You have got Craig Heatley—Craig Heatley—who is completely asleep at the wheel,
completely asleep—[ Interruption] Sorry, Phil Heatley. Phil Heatley. Even Phil—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: Phil Heatley says he agrees with everything, and does
absolutely nothing. He agreed with everyt hing in the poverty report, and what did he
do? He cut funding to community housin g. He cut funding for State house
maintenance—[Bell rung]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Before I call the Hon Bill English, the level of interjection—
actually the level of noise—was discourteous. I hate interrupting members speaking, but
it is so discourteous to have a high level of background noise.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I have not yet met the
housing Minister, Craig Heatley, but I am looki ng forward to meeting the leader of the
Labour Party, Ian Shearer! At least he might get listened to by his front bench when he
gives a speech. It is absolutely clear that even if Charles Chauvel was here yesterday, he
should have been at the barbecue with the Davids, who were not here, because he did
not start listening until the 4 th minute of the speech. No doubt  half of that caucus are
sitting there thinking it is almost the second or  third to last general debate speech that
the current leader of the Labour Party will give.
Yesterday they were away pl otting. What else would Da vid Parker, David Cunliffe,
and Grant Robertson be doing, if they were not in the House on a Tuesday?
[Interruption] Well, Grant Robertson was probably on Skype—I will give you that—
from New York, or wherever he was. I will tell you what they were talking about: the
same things that New Zealand’s union leader ship is talking about in the Koru lounge,
and that is who it is going to be to follow on from David Shearer.
7 Nov 2012 General Debate 6363
The Labour Party should do what it did w ith Helen Clark. Helen Clark was polling
very poorly, making no impact on politics, and Labour stuck with her. In fact, it stuck
with her for 2½ years until  the 1996 election campaign, when she finally came through
to show her political capacities in that cam paign. She still lost the election, polling only
28 percent, but Labour kept backing her. That is when the Labour Party used to
understand middle New Zealand, because it kn ew that in the long run it had a leader
who could take it to victory. This La bour Party does not understand middle New
Zealand, and that is why Labour members are looking to jump ship. The rats are leaving
the ship because David Shearer  does not look like he has b eaten the Government this
year. In just a matter of a few months since he  has been the leader, they are ready to slit
his throat, stab him in the back, and throw him to the wolves. But that is the easy bit.
The hard bit is deciding who w ould replace him. My advice is  that that fight will be so
divisive that they should st ick with David Shearer like they did with Helen Clark,
because he has not all of the same qualities but some of the same qualities.
I would say that he alone, of those on the front bench of Labour, has an instinct for
middle New Zealand. There are other peopl e there who do not, like the Hon David
Cunliffe, who has said publicly—and I think this is honest—in the Listener: “I think I
am sincere.” I think I am sincere! Well, ask anybody who has listen ed to this man—he
is not sincere. He has perfected the ar t, as Mike Moore said—when you can fake
sincerity, you have really got them. But at least David Cunliffe recognises his inner
troubles—and this is not an inner struggle that David Shearer has—when he says that he
has to keep reminding himself that it is not about him, every day: “Every day I look in
the mirror and I tell myself, it is not about me.” Well, the leadership of what used to one
of New Zealand’s fine political parties cannot be about an ego that big.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Bill knows a lot about leadership!

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I do know. I have been there. I know what it feels like. I
know how David Shearer feels today, when he can hear them baying for his blood,
knowing he is going to be cu t down. It is just a matter of  when, because this is the
Labour Party at its best. The discipline it ha d under Helen Clark is gone; now it is egos,
now it is each man for himself, and now La bour members spend a lot more time talking
about themselves than they do—

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Of course, Bill English knows a lot
about leadership, because he was “Mr 22 Percent”, who took the National Party to one
of the worst defeats that it ever had. He is still bitter about it, he is sti ll whinging about
it, and he is still plotting at every moment how he can get back into the Prime Minister’s
seat.
Last week the long-awaited affordable housing package from the Government was
announced. You know, it reminded me of that  old Peggy Lee song from the late 1960s,
“Is That All There is?”. If you remember, Mr Speaker—and I am sure you do—it was a
song about disillusionment. I have to say that New Zealanders who have been waiting
and wishing and hoping for a response to th e growing housing crisis in New Zealand
have every right to feel di sillusioned. Seven months ago the Government received a
report from the Productivity Commission on a ffordable housing. What did that report
do? It set out the issues, it highlighted areas  for action, and it gave the Government 33
recommendations. For 7 months we had to wait for the Government’s response. For 7
months we got the old po litical striptease from the Minist er of Finance: a little speech
here, a little hint of action over there, a patsy question or two in Parliament, and some
pathetic comments like “We clearly have a problem in Auckland with a lack of supply
of housing, particularly for low-income people.  We are determined to get a better deal
for people.”
6364 General Debate 7 Nov 2012
I say to Bill English that he is either not determined enough, or he is a spent force in
the National Cabinet, because he has been overtaken by the ideas man, the apparatchik
of the National Party, Steven Joyce. The affo rdable housing package is toothless, and it
is gutless. As John Armstrong wrote in the New Zealand Herald last week, “Package?
What package?”. I have to agree with him. He said that the Government’s plan looks
like a first draft. Duncan Garner on his blog wrote that “There is nothing bold in here at
all.” [Interruption] Oh, so they are now laughing at D uncan Garner. This is a man they
all suck up to most of the time. They do not like it when he writes the truth. He said that
“it is tinkering while Auckland burns in the face of unsustainable house prices.” He said
that National “has shied away from getting hands on or even getting its hands dirty.” He
said that there was one word for it: underwhelming.
What I say is that it is ti nkering by muddled thinkers de void of ideas, paralysed by
ideology, lacking in vision and innovation, and into a whole lot of blame shifting. Local
government, they say, must stump up, or else. We do not know what the “or else” is, but
local government is being told it must stum p up and address affordable housing in New
Zealand. Of course, the irony of that is that at  the same time that Bill English is saying
that, Nick Smith and his would-be Minister  of Local Government , David Carter, are
saying “No, no, local government, you must get out of anything the private sector could
do.” Well, I can say that this is a pathetic  response to a very serious problem in New
Zealand. We have been told that there will have to be more inquiries, more work done,
and more evaluations.
There is a choice the Government can make . There are two paths a Government can
go down. One is where it is hand s-off, with an approach of  “Business knows best” and
letting the market rule; a deregulated ec onomy, deregulated safety, and deregulated
everything. We are seeing the results in New Z ealand after two decades or more of that
approach, with some of the worst health and safety records around the world, with leaky
buildings, and with a deregulated electricity market that they said would give us cheaper
prices, but which means we are paying more. Then there is the other path a Government
could go down; a Government that is more hands-on, that is supporting its exporters,
that is protecting New Zealand jobs, and th at is leading our bui lding of affordable
homes in New Zealand. The Government s hould be leading by example. An example
was in Hobsonville. What did it do? It can celled affordable housing, and it cancelled
State housing. It is devoid of ideas, and nothing in housing will happen under this
Government as long as it occupies the Treasury benches.

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: We all know the clichés about being in
Opposition, and they all add up to one and the sa me thing—it is not a pretty place to be.
It is particularly difficult when you are in Opposition when you are clearly facing an
internal leadership crisis of the type that  Mr English has just outlined—when the Green
Party is eating your lunch at the same time.
It is perfectly clear what has happened. There has been some type of strategy meeting
and somebody has come up with a “bright idea”. The bright idea is “Let’s declare there
is an economic crisis—a crisis in manuf acturing”, and everyone who is desperate for
something other than another silly proposal to print money has said “What a brilliant
idea! We’ll hold a conference, we’ll paper ove r our cracks, and we’ll declare there’s a
crisis.”
The only problem is that you cannot declare a crisis. You cannot create a crisis by
political fiat. It is particularly difficult to say that New Zealand is facing a crisis when
you are facing the following economic realities. No. 1 is the cost of living. The rate of
inflation has fallen from 5.1 percent in Nove mber 2008 to the lowest rate this century,
taking pressure off New Zealand families, New Zealand households, and New Zealand
7 Nov 2012 General Debate 6365
companies trying to compete everywhere. It is very difficult to say you are facing a
crisis.
It is very difficult to say you are facing a crisis in manufacturing when you have just
seen a Government oversee the creation of 60,000 ne t jobs in the last 2 years. It is very
difficult to say that you are facing a crisis when the Government that replaced you was
facing forecast unemployment going up to 10 percent and it is now —still higher than
we all want it to be, and it is a very challe nging situation—around 6.8 percent. It is very
difficult to say that there is a crisis f acing middle New Zealand when the average New
Zealand household with a $200,000 mortgage is facing a mortgage bi ll that is $200 a
week after tax lower than they were paying in April 2008. That is $200 in the hand. It is
very difficult to persuade those folks that they are facing a cris is. The superannuation
married rate is 22 percent higher than it was in April 2008.
It is very difficult—if we move to the macroeconomic front—to say that New
Zealand is facing a crisis when the current annual growth rate is  2.6 percent and when
you look across the developed world and look at  that in comparison with what other
countries that also enjoy a high standard of  living are facing at the moment. Net Crown
debt, which was forecast when we came to Go vernment to rise above 60 percent, and
deficits thereafter, is now forecast to around 30 percent. That is when the UK itself is
looking at net Crown debt of 85 percent of GDP.
It is very difficult to sustain a manufactured  crisis in the face of economic facts like
those. Let me try to illustrate what would represent a real crisis—a real crisis. We do not
have to invent one, unfortunate ly. We have only to look at eurozone countries and, to
some extent, see what emerges in the United States to understand what a real crisis is. A
real crisis is when you are sitting on eurozone unemployment of over 11 percent—
almost, just a tad short of, twice New Zeal and’s unemployment rate. A real crisis is
when you have got within the eurozone  a 25-plus percent general level of
unemployment in the fourth-largest econom y in the eurozone and you have got 50
percent youth unemployment—people between 15 and 24. One in two of them is unable
to find a future for themselves. That is not just an economic crisis, that is not even just a
social crisis; that could have long-term ex traordinarily serious po litical consequences
for the stability of those places.
That is what a real crisis looks like, not this manufactur ed crisis designed to paper
over the Opposition’s internal difficulties. A real crisis is when the Government is not
following the sorts of policie s that this Government is  following—steady, disciplined
control over public expenditure , nothing extreme, designed to help hard-pressed New
Zealanders take the edges o ff the recession and manage us  all through this extremely
difficult patch internationally, which is facing all countries in the world. When you are
looking at massive cuts in welfare and h ealth services, and 500,000 jobs in the UK
public sector to be slashed in the next 4 years, that is a re al crisis, not the phoney crisis
that the Opposition is trying to paper over.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Later tonight my bill to almost halve
child poverty, the Income Ta x (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment
Bill, will have its vote in the House. I wa nt to thank all those community organisations,
Every Child Counts, the Child Poverty Action Group, Champions for Children, and
many other groups and individuals who ha ve written and emailed, tweeted and
facebooked, marched, rallied, and otherwise worked to have this bill pass its first
reading tonight.
It is with genuine sorrow that I report th at we are still yet to find the one more vote
we need to send this bill to the Social Se rvices Committee. All those parties supporting
the bill tonight have been given a pair of infant socks—baby socks—as a small gesture
from me to acknowledge their commitment to finding a real solution to the poverty that
6366 General Debate 7 Nov 2012
is suffered by a quarter of a million children in New Zealand today. I have one pair of
baby socks left, because we need only one vote from one party to pass the bill. That one
vote will bring the family income of an  estimated 100,000 New Zealand children above
the poverty line. That one vote will ensure th at these children have a warm, dry home,
shoes on their feet, and food in their bellies.
Many organisations have expressed their distress at Peter Dunne’s decision to oppose
my bill. During the 2011 election he signed a pledge with a group called Closer

items.speaker: Together Whakatata Mai. That pledge sa ys
items.text: “As a politician, I choose to commit to
building a fairer New Zealand and will ac tively support policy measures that reduce
income inequality and bring people closer t ogether.” At the time, Peter Dunne wrote: “I
very much support your call for more detail ed debate around the possible ways to
reduce poverty and income inequality.” I ask Peter Dunne to honour tonight that pledge
he made. In a Facebook post in response to my bill, Peter Dunne has said: “I believe
there needs to be recognition of the hard-w orking efforts of low income families, and
the existing In-work Tax Credit is a way of ach ieving that.” It is a way, but it is a way
that discriminates against the poorest families. My bill will remove that injustice and
reduce poverty and income inequality, which he said he wants to achieve.
I have offered Peter Dunne and the Nati onal Government two compromises on my
bill in order to meet their concerns. The first offer was to retain the hours worked
criteria so that all parents who work w ould receive the in-wor k tax credit. At the
moment, if you work and you receive a benef it, superannuation, or a student allowance,
that work goes unrecognised. Mr Dunne has said that he believe s in recognising the
hard-working efforts of low-income families,  but he has refused to recognise the hard-
working efforts of this group of low-in come families—some 40,000 DPB recipients
who work, and another 20,000 who will be expect ed to work at least 15 hours a week
next year. They all go unrecognised by Peter Dunne.
I have also offered an amendment to th e Government and Peter Dunne that would
allow a family to retain the in-work tax credit for 6 months after they lose a job or have
insufficient paid hours. The working adults would then still be incentivised to find a job
or more hours within the 6-month time fram e, but they and thei r children would not
suffer such a severe financial disaster at the time they lose their job, because families
who lose their jobs also lose this tax cr edit. When the job loss has resulted from a
factory closing, like in Mata ura, or a workplace accident, which affects thousands of
New Zealanders every year, or a natural disast er, as we have seen in this country, the
personal and financial strain for those hard-working families is enormous. One vote is
all that those families need.
But I must confess that these compromises I offered to Peter Dunne to meet his—
what I consider to be somewhat irrational —needs were hard to stomach in the offering,
because the Green Party believes that hard-working families are also those who care for
their kids, whether in paid work or not . Hard-working parents are those who are
deserving of dignity and decent treatment b ecause they care for their kids. One vote is
all that these families need. One vote is all that their children need. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Well, we know something is up,
because Mr Cunliffe is growing his bear d again and Mr Jones has had a fresh new
haircut. The last time that happened there was some movement over on the other side.
Have a look, Mr Speaker. Mr Jones has had a nother haircut, and Mr Cunliffe is once
again growing his beard. Something is up.
Of course, I do not know what is going on in the Opposition, because a couple of
weeks ago there was a manufacturing cris is, apparently. Then we showed the
Opposition the numbers and it realised th ere was not a manufacturing crisis. Today
Opposition members are talking about a supposed housing crisis, and the Acting
7 Nov 2012 General Debate 6367
Minister of Housing pointed out today that  there are 634-odd more State houses than
there were when we came in to Government in 2008. I am not sure what the next crisis
is, but, apparently, I do suspect happily that it is there to tr y to cast a shadow or avoid
the leadership crisis under David Shearer. To be  fair to him, he has had a bit of a rough
year. His 1 year is not quite up—I think he has got 20 or so days to go—but the knives
are being sharpened. We watched the leader’s  lead-off debate at general debate time,
and it was very revealing to see those who were not paying any attention whatsoever.
I will move on to the coalition of the unwilling presenting its solutions recently—
Labour and the Greens. Future Minister of Finance, apparently, Russel Norman, will be
casting aside Mr Cunliffe and casting aside Mr Parker, perhaps. Who would be the
Minister of Finance under the coalition of the unwilling over there? But that team has
given us some insights into Labour’s deep thinking. Mr Pa rker, Mr Cunliffe, and Mr
Norman want to fix our exchange rate. They want to fix it at a ce rtain rate. No one has
actually asked them what rate is the correct  rate. No one has actually asked them how
much capital should be put at risk to defend th e exchange rate at a certain level and for
how long. No one has asked them how much capital should be diverted from schools,
hospitals, health, and superannua tion to be used to defend so me artificial exchange rate
that they think is correct. Those questions will be asked, and they will be very revealing
because, once again, those members’ rhetoric  and their grabbing for headlines do not
actually match reality.
The only other solution they have got out ther e that they have told us about is that
they just want to print mone y. It is a fair enough response,  I suppose, which they keep
coming out with day after day when we challenge them—“How will you pay for your
promises?”—that they are just going to ge t the xerox out and th e printing press out.
What a solution! I do not know why after hundreds of years we did not think of that—
why standard, normal economics did not think of that. But, incidentally, there are
examples around the world where they have tried that, and our Prime Minister Key
pulled out some Zimbabwe money the other day to demonstrate that to us.
There is no crisis. New Zeal and is performing in growth statistics better than anyone
else in the OECD right now—better than anyone  else—so there is no crisis. The dream,
or the nightmare, team over there want to abandon our inflation vigilance. Abandoning
our inflation vigilance, which has been stab le for so many years, is like throwing the
sprinklers out or turning the sprinklers off because there has not been a fire in the house.
It is the vigilance, the prudence, of our Public Finance Act and of our Reserve Bank,
and its independence, that have served this country so well and have, essentially, created
so many jobs.
I want to quickly bring us to Hawke’s Bay. Hawke’s Bay has great proposals in front
of it—a huge storage dam to help our economy and to create jobs for our families. I
challenge the Labour Party to put on record whether it supports that proposal, because
its potential coalition partners  are doing all they can to di srupt that proposal. That is
about 3 percent or 4 percent growth for Hawke’s Bay if the dam goes ahead. Eugenie
Sage from the Green Party was sacked afte r 19 years of not ha ving a water plan in
Canterbury and is trying to disrupt the water plan of Hawke’s Bay. I challenge the
Labour Party to say where it stands, because Damien O’Connor said when he was in the
Hawke’s Bay that he supported it, yet one of  its candidates is now  saying that they do
not support it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: What candidate? We don’t have candidates.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: Former candidate, former  MP Ms King. The Opposition
party—it says no to everything. It says no to every initiative to create jobs that grow real
growth and real after-tax incomes. It says no to every Better Public Services
announcement or change we try to put in place.  It says no to families’ aspirations of a
6368 General Debate 7 Nov 2012
brighter future. I am so surprised we have to  fight for so many of the initiatives that we
try to put in place for a much better, brighter future for all of our families in Hawke’s
Bay and beyond.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: There is only one thing worse, as Oscar Wilde said,
than being talked about, and that is not be ing talked about. All th e Government can do
today is talk about the Opposition, talk abou t the Labour Party. Actually, it is only the
Opposition coming up with new ideas to deal with the very serious problems that this
country is facing. The Government has no ideas. Worse than having no ideas, it is out of
touch. This is the Government of Jim Callaghans—the new Jim Callaghans. “What
crisis? There is no crisis.” There is a crisis. There is a crisis in manufacturing. In the last
5 years 40,000 jobs have gone, and export cap acity is reduced. Gone. Fewer of them.
That is why we are struggling. There is a cr isis in manufacturing, and this Government
has got no answer to it.
But the other big crisis in this country—w hich even Tim Groser cannot see, because
he spends far too much time out of this country—is in housing. The Government’s own
report, the Government’s own Productivity Commission, said there is a crisis in
housing, an affordability crisis. Housing is ab solutely essential to a healthy community
and a healthy life. Everybody n eeds a roof over thei r heads, and this  Government has
got no answer to the growing number, the thousands of people, who are increasingly
finding it difficult not even to buy a house but to rent one, because the prices are going
through the roof. The Government  is out of touch and hous ing is out of reach to a
growing number of New Zealanders. The is sue is about affordability. It is about
affordability, but also it is about access to housing—to social housing, to rental
housing—because there has been a run down in rental stock.
You see, I was in New Plymouth just a few days ago with our housing spokesperson,
Annette King, and we went up to the site of a Labour project there to develop housing—
State housing, rental housing, affordable housi ng. It was a project al l ready to go in
2008, and no sooner did this Government get in, it shelved it. It is in an area called
Discovery Place. You know, there is a song that goes along the lines of: “Can we do
what they do on the Discovery Channel?”. Well, in New Plymouth the song is: “Can
you not do what they do on Discovery Place?”, because it is doing absolutely nothing. It
took all the houses away because it told peopl e it was going to redevelop them. It let
what housing was there run dow n. There are only a few tena nts there. They live in
substandard housing. They have no idea wh at is going on because nobody tells them.
Nobody tells them what is going on in Discovery Place, and they need to know.
What is the Government’s answer? The Productivity Commission tells it that there is
an affordability problem. The Government’s own department tells it that there is a
housing problem, and what is the Government ’s answer? Nothing. No plan. No answer.
Fiddle a bit around the edges of planning. Tell the local authorities that they have got to
pull up their act, but what is it doing to the local authorities? It is trying to take away
their powers, because local government under this Government will have no
responsibility for social issues, for broader economic issues, or anyt hing else. What the
left hand wants to do, th e right hand says it is  not going to do. That  is the problem with
this Government: no coherence, no consistency, and no plan.
Actually, a lot more needs to be done. It is  not just about the bu ilders; it is about
those who want to get into housing too—those w ho want to rent at an affordable level,
those who want to buy at an affordable level, those people whose dreams and
aspirations, young people in particular, ar e built on getting on the first rung on the
ladder of housing, and they cannot get ther e. The average price of a house now in
Auckland is $600,000. The average nationally is $360,000. It is impossible for people to
7 Nov 2012 General Debate 6369
get in a house. What is this Government’s plan for housing? There is not one—there is
not one.
There is a lot more that we could be doi ng. What about interven ing in the lending
market? What about the State playing a role as  we used to with th e old State Advances
Corporation? Why do we not assist young people?

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: For goodness’ sake.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Mr Joyce says: “For goodness’ sake.”, because he does not
want to, because those members have no pl an. They will talk about the Labour Party
and they will talk about the Greens and everybody else. They have to because they have
got no plan of their own, because they do not want to help people. They do not want to
help people. They have never cared about people who are finding it tough and who just
want to get ahead. They do not want to help them; they want to help their rich mates.
That is what this Government is about. That is why it does not care about housing and it
does not care about the jobs people are in. It does not even see a problem in
manufacturing, because that is th e nature of it. That is the na ture of it. It does not see a
problem when there is one. More has to be done. This Government is doing nothing and
this country is crying out for an action pl an. A decent housing plan would create jobs
and would stimulate the economy, but this Government will not do it, because it has run
out of ideas, it has run out of steam, and all it can do is point the finger at other people.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: A couple of weeks ago I had cause to go to
the dictionary after an inte rjection by David Parker on th e Prime Minister, when the
Prime Minister was talking about jobs in ma nufacturing. Mr Parker interjected that the
figure that the Prime Minister was using in cluded agriculture and therefore it somehow
did not count as manufacturing. So I we nt to Wikipedia and I found that, indeed,
manufacturing is the production of goods or services. It could be handicraft to high tech,
but it is certainly not limited to steel construc tion. But that seems to be the attitude of a
certain member from Dunedin—the negativ e, down in the mouth, glass half-empty
member for South Dunedin—because when we we nt to Dunedin last week she issued a
press release, before we had even done anything, actually, saying that Key had front to
go down to Dunedin and suggest that there was no manufacturing crisis. In fact, he
never said any such thing in all of that  trip, but what we did do, I think, was
acknowledge that there are challenges in manufacturing.
But the Government does not have the luxury of focusing on just the negative things.
It actually has that tough job of focusing on the positive things th at are going on in the
manufacturing industry. On Tuesday, with Da vid Carter, I met with some exporters in
Dunedin and also the owner of Cowell’s Ge nuine Pavlova. This is a great little
organisation in Dunedin that I claim make s the best pavlovas in the country. My
colleague Craig Foss—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s true.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, my colleague Craig Foss actually disagrees with
me, but I would suggest that Cowell’s is th e No. 1, and it would normally employ about
eight people. At the moment, to manage the Christmas rush, it has 21 staff madly filling
the orders, and most of those pavlovas ar e going to end up in Australia. Talk about
selling coals to Newcastle! This great li ttle company is now exporting pavlova to
Australia.
The Prime Minister and I started our trip la st week at a great wee company in North
Taieri, the New Zealand Honey Co. Faced with competition from bulk commodity
product coming in from China, it had a choice. It could either compete, add value, or
fold, and it decided to compete. It is a Deloitte Fast 50 winner from 2009 or 2010, and it
is now exporting millions of dollars’ worth of value-added honey products into the UK
and China.
6370 General Debate 7 Nov 2012
We then went on and visited Speights Brewery, that great brewery in Dunedin. While
the Canterbury earthquake rebuild posed so me serious challenges for the Dunedin
workforce in losing its workers, at Speights it is going the other way. There are actually
workers coming down from Canterbury Draught and millions of dollars being invested
in the production line at Speights Brewery, and I understand it has announced just today
the takeover of Emerson’s Brewery, a fant astic boutique brewer y in Dunedin. That
could create export opportunities. What it will certainly do is put capital into the city for
those fantastic people, the Emersons, to l ook at other investment opportunities. And we
did go to some steel manufacturing. We went to Farra’s, a 140-year-old company—

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: Are they busy?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Yes, they are. They are struggling, but they are
growing in revenue, they are growing jobs, and they are growing new markets. When
the PM asked them: “If the challenges f aced by the Hillside workshops resulted in
further job losses, would they and the engine ering cluster in Dunedin be able to pick
them up?”, the simple answer was: “Absol utely, yes.” So manufacturing is not just
about steel, and certainly, in Dunedin, it is not just about what is done in Hillside Road.
But I will say this about the member for Dunedin South. She has come out in support
of responsible oil and gas expl oration in the southern Canterbury Bight off the coast of
Dunedin.

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: Really?

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, it is no t surprising that you would say
“Really?”, because she has been very quiet about it. No ads in the paper the way the rest
of the chamber of commerce members were doing, welcoming Anadarko. No bold
statements that say, yes, there could be challenges at Hillside, but there are also
opportunities in the city. None of that, but she has quietly said that, yes, she does
support oil and gas exploration. I think she needs to be brav er about that and do what
the other city leaders in Dunedin and the other MPs—certainly, the National MPs in the
south, Jacqui Dean and myself—are doing and say to Anadar ko and Shell: “Bring it on.
Explore. Do it responsibly, do it safely, but certainly contribute to the manufacturing
and export opportunities that do exist in Dunedin, despite the challenges.”

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: The people who created a society of equals in
New Zealand would be sickened  and disgusted at what sort  of country we now live in.
New Zealand is now a land of the haves and the have-nots. We are on the path towards
creating a State-sponsored slave colony.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, for goodness’ sake! Ha, ha! You clown.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: The number of people at the bottom of the heap is
growing. The Hon Steven Joyce can smile and laugh, but the number of people at the
bottom of the heap is growing. Those at the top are getting richer and richer, helped by
huge tax cuts from this National Government . This is a low-wage , high-price economy.
That is what National and its big business backers want. They want queues of workers
standing in the cold, begging for jobs. They  want a minimum wage economy and even
less for the youth of this country—even less than the minimum wage.
Many New Zealanders are leav ing the country as the Government continues its job
eradication programme. Recently, at Victoria University, some 200 students were asked
the question “What are you planning to do when you finish your degree?”, and some
170 of the 200 in the group said “We’re goi ng to go and live overseas. There is no
future in this country with the qualifications that we have.” Is that not sad when 170 out
of 200 young people feel that the future for th em is not in this country? Yet National
and its friends are bringing in thousands of immigrants  to keep pushing down the
wages—advertising in the likes of the UK fo r workers to come to Christchurch, while
we have people unemployed and while we have something like 6.8 percent
7 Nov 2012 General Debate 6371
unemployment. It is interesting that Tim Groser mentioned befo re that in Europe
unemployment is at 11 percent and we are not even halfway there at 6.8 percent. Well,
that particular Minister really cannot do his maths very well, because he said we were
virtually half of Europe. Well, 6.8 percent is not half of 11 percent, Minister.
The wages at the top keep soaring, as evid enced this week in the headline “Rise of
the $1m salaries: top boss says enough”. More  than 41 senior executives are getting
more than $1 million in this country, many of whom are simply not worth that sort of
money. The real wages at the bottom and th e benefits keep fa lling. Rampant capitalism
is now a disease, and it has infected  many countries thro ughout the world. Greedy
financiers and bankers have destroyed en tire economies, many of whom have been
bankers in the likes of Merrill Lynch in  New York in their previous lives. The
Government’s own figures released today sh ow that its tired ol d slash-and-burn-and-
sell-out policies are not working. The tax ta ke is down. The deficit is growing. Every
day there is a sad story of another failure.
The Government’s only solution is to sell our precious assets overseas and to make
us a colony of China and everywhere else where the economy is controlled. This is a
