those heritage buildings as well. Perhaps now he will have the time to see that done.
7 Nov 2012 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 6391
It is particularly frustrating when you see that about $196 million was spent on
making Eden Park in Auckland a place that was fit to host the Rugby World Cup. What
a great sporting event that was last year. But in Christchurch we have seen less than $10
million from the Government put into s upporting the retention, making safe, and
repairing of our heritage buildings. It ju st does not weigh up, in my view. Once those
heritage buildings are lost, we cannot recap ture them. We cannot suddenly recreate the
decades and decades of architectural commitme nt that we have seen from them over
that past time, let alone the emotional commit ment that people have to their buildings.
We have many that are going. The Lyttelton Tunn el control building is the latest one to
have the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority sign-off for demolition. It is one of
Peter Beaven’s buildings, one that  is not particularly attractiv e, actually, but that is not
the point of architecture; it is what it repres ents in our time-scale of architectural design
and ability and commitment in our region. That  is another building that is going to be
lost for the sake of just a couple of million dollars.
I am very supportive of this bill. I look fo rward to that vision and that time now
being made by the member for the rest of the historic structures in our region, which are
worthy of that same support.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: There is much of what Ruth Dyson
said about the importance of Riccarton Bush  to the heritage of Christchurch and
Canterbury with which I agree. That is why the Local Government and Environment
Committee unanimously recommended that this Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill, in the
name of the Hon Gerry Brownlee, the memb er of Parliament for Ilam, have broad
support.
I think we should at this stage of the bill ’s debate, in the third reading, acknowledge
the huge heritage that goes with the Deans family 169 year s ago in building the initial
buildings that are part of that which is protected, and the step 98 years ago, back in
1914, when it was gifted for the benefit of the people of Christchurch and Canterbury. It
is truly a national icon and a treasured ar ea. This bill quite sensibly updates the
governance arrangements for that Riccarton Bush area.
I want to join with other members and ac knowledge the work of  the trustees of
Riccarton Bush, and the work that they have put into this bill. I acknowledge that the
member of Parliament for Ilam, Gerry Brow nlee, is actually a former trustee of
Riccarton Bush. I think the—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: And former chairman.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: A chair, I am told, of Riccart on Bush. I correct that. I also
want to acknowledge that the stand of kahika tea trees that is in Riccarton Bush is a
reminder of the forest that once covered the bulk of the Canterbury plains. It is of huge
significance as part of the na tural heritage. I think that at a time when, tragically, so
many Christchurch buildings have been da maged, we all are relieved that those
buildings that go back to 1843 in Riccarton Bush, including the homestead, which was
built in the 1850s and parts of  it in 1900, have been able to  survive the earthquake. On
those things I agree, and there is consensus.
I do, though, find some of Ruth Dyson’s commen ts about the broader heritage issues
in Christchurch, in respect of the enormous challenge for my colleague Gerry Brownlee
around the earthquake recovery, a bit off beam. You see, like so many areas that we see
from the Opposition, you would think that the New Zealand Government has a blank
cheque. If Labour’s position truly is as Ruth  Dyson expresses, and that is that every
heritage building in Christchurch is goi ng to be protected and built, then I say—
[Interruption] I see the Greens are interjecting. Ever y single debate we hear in this
House you literally would think that money gr ows on trees. In fact I say to the Green
6392 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
Party—the Green Party actually proposed to print money. I am just pleased that the Hon
Gerry Brownlee is not in that camp, that he is realistic and realises there are balancing—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: You are wrong, wrong, wrong. Wrong.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: You are not going to print money?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Wrong.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: They are not going to print money. Well, I actually
specifically heard the members—the leader of the party—say that they are going to
print money to be able to rebuild all the her itage in Christchurch. I would simply say to
the Green Party, if the proposals that I have heard that every single piece of heritage in
Christchurch can simply be protected by printing money are not—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Is that what Ruth Dyson said? Is that what she said?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: No, I was referring to the interjection from the Green Party.
What I would say to Ruth Dyson, and to the member who has just interjected, is show
us the money. Show us the money. If you are going to go around the people of
Christchurch and say that you are going to pr otect—and the latest we have had is the
tunnel building at Lyttelton—I simply ch allenge members opposite, show us how you
are going to pay for it. The last thing the pe ople of Christchurch and Canterbury need is
the hollow promises from Labour members around heritage.
I want to simply commend the very real istic and practical approach that Gerry
Brownlee has taken around that hugely difficult  issue of the heritage  that we are going
to protect, to making buildings safe, and the $6 billion of public  money that Gerry
Brownlee has secured for the people of Christc hurch in the rebuild of that great city.
This bill is a sensible bill, which will  mean that generations of the people of
Christchurch and Canterbury will be able to  enjoy both the histor ic heritage and the
natural heritage that is Riccarton Bush. I commend the local member for the work that
he has done with this bill, and the trustees  of Riccarton Bush, who have put the work
into it, and I join with the select committee in  saying this is a bill of which Parliament
should be proud and that we should get on and pass.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I stand to support the
Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill. It is a good bill. It is well supported by the House, and
I want to thank the member Gerry Brownlee for bringing it here.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: The Green Party is pleased  to support this bill, the
Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill, but I join with my colleague Ruth Dyson, the member
for Port Hills, in expressing some puzzlemen t over the way in which the Minister, in a
very eloquent speech today, described, with a huge amount of knowledge and
enthusiasm and passion, the he ritage values of Riccarton Bu sh, the buildings there, and
the forest, and yet he is the same member w ho called heritage buildings in Christchurch
“old dungers” and who, in his role as the Minister responsible for the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority, has seen the demolition of much of the heritage
character of Christchurch.
So what we are seeing here in this bill is the protection and the retention of Riccarton
Bush, Riccarton House, and Deans Cottage, improved governance arrangements for that
area, and an improved management plan regime and criteria for Riccarton Bush, but that
same care and attention is not being applied to the rest of our heritage character in
Christchurch. There we see a very aggressive demolition strategy by the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority. It  is tragic that we do not have that same stewardship
that we are showing and the Riccarton Bush Trust has shown through its trust deed and
its care and stewardship of Riccarton Bush gi ven to heritage in Christchurch, because it
is not just about the cost in  terms of dollars. It was th e vision of the Deans family,
which set aside the forest and the buildings at Deans Bush for the people of
Christchurch. We need to show that same  vision in protecti ng the character of
7 Nov 2012 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 6393
Christchurch, which attracts visitors to the city and which is part of the city’s identity,
because by safeguarding that, we safeguard part of the city’s economy. By destroying
heritage, we create a wasteland in the city—an expanse of gravel, concrete, and
desolation, and a city that has no heart.
We need to show that same care that we are giving to Riccarton Bush to the
remaining heritage buildings in the city. If we are talking about money, $10 million has
been given to heritage buildi ngs in Christchurch, and half of that to the Arts Centre.
Worthy, yes, but we need to increase that p ūtea so that we can encourage owners who
want to conserve their buildings, like th e NG building on Madras Street, which is
threatened by the authority’s blueprint for the central city. There are a lot of owners who
want to keep their buildings.
The New Zealand Transport Agency needs to  be encouraged to protect the Lyttelton
Tunnel building. It is using the rockfall risk to say that the building must be demolished.
Well, if it is rockfall, why is the State highway and the access to Lyttelton Tunnel not
closed to protect people travelling on that road every day?
This is a good bill, but the sentiments of the member who has sponsored it, which are
very valuable, need to be reflected and carried  over to the protecti on of our heritage in
the city, so that we have a city that has char acter, that people want to continue to visit,
and that has an identity that has been established in part through its heritage buildings.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : Deans Bush, with its remnant of kahikatea forest,
and the Deans homestead since 1843 have be en a very important Christchurch city
asset, one of many such assets in Christch urch, that should be preserved for future
generations. Its importance is in the bush area itself—the last kahikatea remnant in the
built-up area of the city—in the house, with its Victoria n wooden architecture, and, of
course, in its being an important part of the history of the city, ha ving originally been
the Deans homestead. This property has been well cared for, but only since about 1990,
using Christchurch City ratepayers’ money, and that needs to continue. This bill, the
Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill, will see that it does.
Before that the property had been in a bad state and the bush had not been well
protected. The early 1990s were the first time that the Christchurch City Council
committed the adequate funding necessary for the preservation of this house and
grounds, including the bush behind it. As a member of the council from 1989 to 2004, I
was one of the councillors who committed voluntarily the funding necessary to make
sure that the past regime of neglect all ch anged, and what we see now is a property that
we can all be proud of, despite the current earthquake damage. During the same period I
was also a member of the Canterbury Mu seum trust board, and that building was
earthquake-strengthened during the same pe riod, especially the 1872 wing. I recall that
it was in a sad state, too. In fact, it was in  such a sad state that a good sneeze, let alone
an earthquake, would have brought down. So a lo t of work and a lot of expense had to
be expended to make sure that it was pr eserved against earthquakes—in particular,
much stronger walls. In addition, I set up a nd chaired a council subcommittee to save
the old Government Building behind Cathedra l Square. In due course it was purchased
by the council for a few hundred thousand do llars. It too was strengthened against
earthquakes and the sprinklers added, and then  it was resold with protective covenants
and is now the Heritage Christchurch hotel.
All these buildings, including Riccarton House,  survived the recent earthquakes with
minor damage, in stark contrast to other Ch ristchurch heritage buildings, and I would
like to mention three of them. First of all, there is the Canterbury Provincial Council
Chambers, which for many years was unde r the wing of the Canterbury Regional
Council, which during those years did absolu tely nothing whatsoever to strengthen it
against earthquakes. The Angli can Cathedral in Ca thedral Square, under its ownership
6394 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
by the Anglican Church property trustees, di d very little to stre ngthen that building
against earthquakes, even though it had been seriously damaged in previous
earthquakes. Obviously, they did not really have the funds necessary for the purpose.
The Arts Centre was an ongoing project fo r earthquake strengthening, and that came
from public funds—mainly Christchurch City  Council funds, too. We did the work as a
council on Riccarton House, the Canterbury Museum, the old Government Building, the
Arts Centre, and other such heritage buildings because we knew, as citizens of
Christchurch, that that work was needed, an d we knew that it wa s valued by the people
of Christchurch and that they would have it fo r posterity. That work has paid off, as is
now evident following the earthquakes. This bill will help to ensure the ongoing
maintenance of Riccarton House and Riccarton Bush.
But what about other Christchurch herita ge buildings? The Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery has powers and the Ca nterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority
has powers under the Canterbury Earthquake Rec overy Act to ensure that buildings like
Riccarton House are preserved and ultimately restored in whole or in part. Heritage
issues are not just the elephant in the ea rthquake recovery room; they are a herd of
mammoths in the room. New Zealand Governments have always been tardy at assisting
with earthquake strengthen ing of heritage buildings, and it is now tardy about
recovering and preserving those buildings mo st needing it. There are many of those. I
have asked questions for written answer of th e Minister in charge of heritage, and got a
worthless, smart-alecky reply, which shows only that he shou ld not be the Minister in
charge of heritage because he clearly has not got a skerrick of interest about the subject
at all. He would be better to resign. That would be the most positive thing he could do. I
understand that the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority has a draft policy on
heritage buildings for Christchurch, and I understand that the Minister is happy for it
now to be released. But why has it not been released, Mr Brownlee? Why has that draft
policy not been released? All Christchurch pe ople want to know what the policy of the
Canterbury Earthquake Recove ry Authority and the Gove rnment is about these
buildings. It is high time we found out from the Minister in charge.
This bill is great for Riccart on House, but what about all the others in much more
urgent need of attention? In particular, wh at about the Christchurch Cathedral? Why is
that different from Riccarton House? Gerry Brownlee has said in answer to a question
for oral answer that it is a matter only for the church, but that is not correct. Like
Riccarton Bush and Riccarton House, for which there is a trust board, there is also one
for the cathedral. So why no action on the mo st important building in the city, the
Christchurch Cathedral? It obviously can be preserved in whole or  in part. The whole
Canterbury community contributed  to its construction and ma intenance, including a lot
of council ratepayer funding. Th e Minister and the Canter bury Earthquake Recovery
Authority must act now to apply the funding th ey have to save the cathedral and in due
course to see that it is restored at least in part.
I and many other Cantabrians want answer s from the Minister on this, not just on
Riccarton House. I and many others want to see the 2003 Act that empowers the
Anglican Church property trustees and covers  the cathedral to be amended, so that in
return for Government funding, and in a ddition to insurance money, donations, and
contributions from elsewhere, there would be an Act very much like the bill now under
discussion covering Riccarton House, so that  the cathedral could then be restored,
owned in trusts for future generations, and used as a multi-faith facility and for concerts
and other public events. If it works for Ricca rton House, it will work for the cathedral.
But instead we have heard nothing but si lence from the Minister and from the
Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority. It is not good e nough. I want to hear now,
and the public wants to hear now , what is going to be done. The alternative is for the
7 Nov 2012 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 6395
cathedral to remain in its current trust and for it to be demolished for want of funding—
a tragedy for Christchurch, Canterbury, a nd New Zealand, and an indictment on this
Government and this generation as a whole.
Returning finally to the Riccarton Bush Am endment Bill now before us, I say that it
should obviously be supported. Reservations th at New Zealand First had when the bill
was first introduced, relating to some aspects of the financial plan, have been solved
with the recent amendments to clause 23( 3). So with those amendments, New Zealand
First is happy to support the bill, but we wait in expectation for what will be done about
the real problem in Christchurch: all of thos e heritage buildings, most particularly the
cathedral, for which we have had nothing but silence, silence, and silence, and for which
action is now needed.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I rise with pleasure to speak to the
third reading of the Riccarton Bush Amendm ent Bill. I have spoken in both the other
readings on this bill, and I woul d like to add to some of the things that I have said, and
to add to some of the speakers. The s ponsoring member, Gerry Brownlee, has so
eloquently set the scene, detailing the colonial history of this family, and I would like to
concentrate more on the natura l heritage that this gives us in terms of a link to
Gondwanaland, which is our link wi th the ancient past. It is a way of preserving as an
open-air plant museum, if you like, a piece of our vegetation and our native heritage that
no longer exists anywhere else in this count ry, let alone in the world, so it must be
preserved. I think that the board, in the way that this bill has been drafted and put
together, will be able to its job properly.
To me, Riccarton Bush represents the very  best of what the original colonial
conservators did. These conservators were well ahead of their time. These were
people—the Deans family and, in particular, the widow, Jane—who showed a
leadership around plants and conservation that  we can all learn from still to this day.
They decided that they would use in a prude nt fashion not only wh at was available to
them to build their houses, to build the buildings that they needed to run a farm, but also
to leave the remnants, because this area, as  has been said, is a swampy area. It had
podocarps in it. The predominant tree was the kahikatea and there was also the mighty
tōtara. These are trees that were felled. They were cut down. Kahikatea itself, which is
called the white pine, a Dacrycarpus, was used primarily and felled in the tens of
thousands of hectares to make butter boxes,  to send our butter to  Europe. Although that
might have been useful at the time, it was a pretty short-sighted thing to do.
The kahikatea, to many of us, is one of the most accessible, I suppose, of our native
trees. They retain a beauty and a majesty th at is perhaps more accessible than some of
the kauri, for example. So when we look at the swampy land in Riccarton Bush, we look
at kahikatea, which was one of the few speci es that would survive in such conditions.
Perhaps because it was swampy, the land was le ft with those trees on it, but that, again,
is the cleverness and the forward thinking of the family. The Deans family decided that
this was something that needed to be preserved because it was of the land. I would
remind people that we have seen in this coun try of ours a lot of trees and a lot of our
native vegetation devastated.
Others have spoken about the colonial her itage, and I am not going to dwell on that,
but I am going to talk about the fossil remains of the trees in Riccarton Bush—remains
that date back 130 million years. This is an open-air museum that gives us a direct link
to our past. It is not very big. It is only 15 acres, and it is the sole remnant of kahikatea
flood plain forest, so it  is a very significant piece of vegetation, not only for the people
of Canterbury but also in th e wider context, and, indeed, in the world context. David
Bellamy, who had a series of television shows through the 1980s and 1990s, came and
6396 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
filmed in Riccarton Bush. He said that this was a living link with our past that must be
preserved in perpetuity.
It is not that we need people to visit us  from overseas to tell us how well we are
doing, but in that instance I think it did gi ve a lot of confidence to the people of
Canterbury that what they were doing, and what Riccarton Bush represented, was
entirely significant, and not just to the pe ople of Canterbury in th eir own area, as the
people who visited there since they were children, who ha d enjoyed going and playing
on the trunks of the trees that had been felled, and who had had a good time. Children
were allowed to wander there free. It was one of the original parks that was enjoyed by
people on their Sunday outings in Christchurch. But further to that, it is an entirely
significant piece of vegetation in the interna tional sense. On a programme I used to
front, Maggie’s Garden Show , we went back and filmed in Riccarton Bush on many
occasions. Again, when you are looking for a place in New Zealand that represents
something that we have lost, we come back time and again to Riccarton Bush, because
it is such a precious place.
I would have to say that the governance stru cture of the board does need assistance,
and, again, I commend the sponsor of this b ill, the Hon Gerry Brownlee. To update the
governance arrangements is to ca rry on that wisdom, that lead ership, that foresight that
was shown by the original Deans family. Thes e are people who are visionaries, but they
need assistance.
I think this cuts across four other bills. It  actually brings together and vests in the
land at 30 Kahu Road, Christchurch, a very  significant group of powers. There are
challenges that exist, really, for this board. What this bill would enable it to do is
actually make some decisions a bout how to preserve  it in the future, to safeguard it,
with management practices that are bold and forward thinking.
Removing native plant species that are not endemic to that piece of land is something
that people in Christchurch have struggled  with, but Diane Lucas and a lot of other
landscape designers have led the charge on this, and at Riccarton Bush they are
contemplating it. It would mean the remova l of exotic conifers. That is a pretty
contentious and controversial thing to do, a nd many say that it should not be done. But
others say it needs to be a pristine piece of bus h. So, really, native plant species need to
be protected. This legislation will allow that to occur, and I commend it to the House.
I know that it will be passed despite some of the cheaper pot-shots from the people
on the other side, who, of course, cannot resist such a thing. But, basically, in the Local
Government and Environment Committee there was a unanimous purpose around this
bill—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Can you blame us? It’s a hell of a target.

items.speaker: MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: —which is not really echoe d by the people who comment now,
like Mr Twyford, who was never there. He knows nothing about it, but blathers on, as is
his wont. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I rise to
make a brief contribution in support of the Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill. May I, as
the opposite and other M āori member for the area in que stion, firstly congratulate the
member for Ilam on bringing this bill to the House. I woul d like to support and
congratulate all of the people who have been involved in bringing this bill to the House.
I would like to thank the member who has ju st resumed her seat, Maggie Barry, for the
history lesson, and for taking us all the way back to G ondwanaland, “Jurassic Park”,
and all the ancient forests that le d, as the excellent chair of the M āori Affairs
Committee, Tau Henare, would sa y, to the tapestry, the bringing together, of so many
rich histories that are embodied in this special area of Riccarton Bush.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: With such eloquence he should be Speaker.
7 Nov 2012 Riccarton Bush Amendment Bill 6397

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Very much so. The leading candidate to be the next Speaker
is the Hon Tau Henare. So there is a rich hist ory there, and I commend this bill. It is a
shame, though, that the bill is being spread over four different Acts of Parliament—or is
soon to be four different Acts of Parlia ment. We have heard members opposite talk
about reducing the amount of legislation, a nd it would have been nice to condense this
into one nice and tidy single piece of legislation.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: That’s what it does. It gets rid of it.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: No, it does not get rid of it, unfortunately. It covers four
pieces of legislation covering over 98 years. Riccarton Bush is a very special place, as
we know. Its history goes back millions of ye ars in terms of its ge ological and natural
beauty, and its historical, and local, and M āori, and colonial history. So I look forward
to seeing the passage of this bill through the House, and I commend it to the House. Kia
ora.
Bill read a third time.
INCOME TAX (UNIVERSALISATION OF IN-WORK TAX CREDIT)
First Reading
Debate resumed from 17 October.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: I am pleased to take a final call on this Income Tax
(Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill from our side. I have had
time to reflect on contributions from member s opposite to this particular bill and this
debate. I must say that when it comes to  child poverty, members who have spoken on
this bill have not displayed any compassi on or understanding or empathy for the plight
of poor families bringing up young children in th is country. They ha ve not done that at
all. In fact, members opposite in the debate 2 weeks ago were actually quite disparaging
of the plight of the poor. Effectively, th ey pathologised that  poverty through their
comments, and I think that was a pretty na sty thing to do. Government members were
effectively saying that there is nothing mo re that can be done for the 270,000 children
who live in poverty, making New Zealand’s pe rformance on this score one of the worst
in the world. We are entitled to draw the conclusion that apart from punitive measures,
which the Government has taken in the last 4 years, it is just not interested in this
particular area. Instead of taking the opportunity to reflect on the reality of these lives of
quiet desperation—because that is what it is; many of these families live lives of quiet
desperation—Government members, instead of  talking about it, have actually gone on
the attack in the debate and indeed in ot her debates concerning this subset of the
population.
David Bennett’s contribution to this debate reached probably even lower than the
lowest, which is usually rese rved for Maggie Barry—apart from the last speech, and I
will acknowledge that. [ Interruption] Well, if the cap fits, wear it. That is saying
something. For David Bennett the provisions of this bill were communism. That is what
he said. Although I doubt he could accurately  define the concept of communism, he
went on to interject that $60 per week will not  make any difference to the lives of these
poor families living in poverty. Clearly, David Bennett was not listening at all to what
the Green members were talking about. Both Metiria Turei and Jan Logie actually gave
examples of what the experience was. Me tiria talked about empty lunch boxes in
schoolbags—$60 would go a long way. Teachers are desperately seeking funds for kids’
breakfasts. There is increasin g illness and kids desperatel y looking for food in places
where animals look for food. Yet those were the disparaging comments that he was
6398 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 7 Nov 2012
making. Jan Logie also talked about the poor being left out, not being able to go on
school trips, feeling the sham e of having no spare resources,  lacking warm clothes, and
living from week to week.
So this is the empathy of the members oppos ite for the poor in this country, the most
vulnerable. For these families, Mr Bennett,  $60 a week would go a very long way. Of
course, it will not go a long way for him, because for him it is only a meal at a
reasonable, mid-range restaurant. But for these families it makes the difference between
living and really being miserable. Paul Goldsmith in his comments on the bill invoked
the spectre of assistance to these families as destroying the human spirit. Which century
is this guy from? The Charity Organisation Society was a long time ago. Assistance, he
said, was like a narcotic. I say to Mr Goldsmith that he cannot hide from these images
he created during the debate, regardless of the fact that the quot e was from someone
who should have known better. But by quoting these lines he associates himself with the
images that this work conjures up.
This bill actually is a good bill. It really addresses the most vulnerable, and the
Government shows a lack of regard. Imagine a family with very little resources bringing
up young children, and young children are our futu re. Yet the Government is miserable
enough to say that we cannot give them that—they will have to get a job and will have
to do something else. Where do members opposite get their knowledge from? What
about the poor in Maungakieki e? What about the poor in Waitakere? What about those
people? Have they not gone and seen them? Ha ve they not talked to those families? Yet
they come here.
The other point I want to make is that for these children this period of development is
the most important there is. If we mess up dur ing those early years,  age 1 to 2, all the
research shows that they are on a downw ard path. But that Government and the
members who spoke on this bill are quite ha ppy for that to happen, yet they privilege
their own; they privilege the rich through tax cuts. I think they have taken a miserable
position, and it will come back to haunt th em. They could have at least shown an
appreciation and voted for this bill to go to the select committee. Thank you.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I want to thank all of those who have
spoken in support of the Income Tax (Unive rsalisation of the In-work Tax Credit)
Amendment Bill over the last few weeks and are voting to send it to the Social Services
Committee. I understand that 60 members of the House tonight will vote in favour of
the bill—very nearly a major ity of Parliament. It is not quite enough but a good start,
and better than we have seen in the past . I want to thank also all of those New
Zealanders who have supported this bill in their various ways, and supported the
campaign to end child poverty.
The Green Party has long believed that the in-work tax credit is unjust. The reasons
for keeping it in its current form are facile. Worse, they damage individual families and
children by trapping them into poverty, and damage community cohesion by creating an
arbitrary and unreal separation between t hose who work and those who rely on a
benefit. It is unjustifiable.
I recently saw two graphs showing the tre nd of child poverty from the mid 1980s to
today from both Australia a nd New Zealand. The New Zeala nd graph is unsurprising.
Child poverty rose radically during the late 1980s and in to the 1990s, particularly
during the National Party’s vicious attacks on beneficiaries. Child poverty reduced
slightly in the 2000s with Working for Families, but it remains worse now than it was in
the 1980s—that is, a greater percentage of chil dren now live in pove rty than did in the
1980s. In Australia over exactly the same period of time, in a similar economy and
culture, the rates of child pov erty have continued to decline and decline. The two
images of New Zealand and Australia child poverty rates are vastly different, because
7 Nov 2012 Income Tax (Universalisation of Tax Credit) Amdt Bill 6399
they tell two different stories about how children are valued in the economy by the
political decision makers.
In Australia there is a comprehensive set of child-related payments of significant
amounts. The payments are for the children and they apply to a family regardless of
whether a person is in work or on a benef it. Australian families get something like
NZ$330 a week for two children aged between 5 and 13, and more if the youngest child
is under 5. If the child is newborn, familie s get a one-off payment of A$5,000 to help
cover the costs.
In New Zealand the same two-child family is subject to highly complex and
discriminatory criteria for Working for Fa milies. They get something like $216 a week
for their children only  if they satisfy hours of work cr iteria and are not on a benefit. If
they are on a benefit, or have simply lost work, they get only $156 a week. Low-income
parents with a newborn in New Zealand who do not meet the stringent requirements for
paid parental leave get, at most, an extr a $1,200 parental tax payment. Parents who are
on a benefit get no extra financial assistance at all for their newborn babies.
In New Zealand families with children have been deliberately stripped of decent
income support either through benefit cuts , deliberate wage-reduc tion policies, or by
discriminatory Working for Families tax transfers that value some families over others.
The name “in-work” for this particular child payment is simply a justification to deny
the child payment to New Zealand’s poores t children. In doing so, the Government
saves itself some $450 million a year. The accumulative loss of income for low-income
households since 2006 is $2.5 billion. That is $2.5 billion that is money taken from the
mouths of New Zealand’s poorest children.
These are political decisions. Solutions to poverty are absolutely determined by
political action to put childre n at the centre of the Govern ment’s economic decisions to
value their dignity and security by guarant eeing the essentials: decent benefits, good
wages, and affordable homes. No provision  of services or charities can eliminate
poverty; it can only help ease the worst effects, and that is desperately needed. But child
poverty is a political issue.  Child poverty is an economi c issue. The Green Party
proudly puts children at the centre of its poli tical and economic decisions. We ask that
this Parliament does the same. I commend this bill to the House.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the Income Tax (Universalisation of
In-work Tax Credit) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.
Ayes 60
New Zealand Labour 34; Green Part y 14; New Zealand First 8; M āori Party 3;
Mana 1.
Noes 61
New Zealand National 59; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Motion not agreed to.
