LOCAL GOVERNMENT (PUBLIC LIBRARIES) AMENDMENT BILL
First Reading

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I move, That the Local Government (Public
Libraries) Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Local Government
and Environment Committee to consider the bill. This bill is about keeping public
library services free for all New Zealanders. The bill would make public library services
a statutory obligation for c ouncils and would make core library services such as
borrowing and internet access free. We have a fine tradition in New Zealand of our local
libraries. We were brought up with them, our  children visit them, new migrant students
and older people rely on them. If members ha ve not visited their local library recently,
they should. They will find vibrant, exciting, and inclusive hubs of community learning
and activity.
I want to acknowledge my colleague Grant Robertson, the original author of this bill.
I was delighted to pick it up from him, a nd even more pleased when it was drawn from
the ballot. I also want to acknowledge the important role of the Library and Information
Association of New Zealand—LIANZA—which has been advocating for legislation of
this type for some time. Its members have b een talking with their local MPs. I am sure
many of you will have heard from these gua rdians of the taonga we call our local
libraries.
Who could ever imagine that our librar ies could be at ri sk? Yet with the
Government’s focus on local government cost-cutting, increasingly strapped local
authorities may turn their attention to library  services and more charges. Despite what
many New Zealanders believe, our public librar ies are not protected in legislation. Our
current legislation only advise s local authorities to ensure local residents can join
libraries free of charge. We are out of step  internationally with  countries such as
Australia, the United Kingdom,  and Canada, all of which protect free public library
services via legislation.
We are not meeting Unesco guidelines where public libraries, in principle, should be
free of charge and the responsibility of lo cal and national aut horities financed by
national and local governments. The Unesco Public Library Manifesto states: “The
public library, the local gate way to knowledge, provides a basic condition for lifelong
learning, independent decision-making and cult ural development of the individual and
social groups. This Manifesto proclaims UN ESCO’s belief in the public library as a
living force for education, culture, and information, and as an essential agent for the
fostering of peace and spiritual welfare through the minds of men and women.” This bill
will help New Zealand meet Unesco guidelines. It will address the issue of user charges
and ensure that New Zealand’s public libraries are an esse ntial component of any long-
term strategy for culture, information provision, literacy, and education.
Over the last couple of months since the bill was drawn, I have reacquainted myself
with my local library. I have visited many ot her libraries and have found they are well
6414 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
attended and supported, sometimes crowded, with an important store of local and family
history and exciting places of  discovery. At the Auckland Ce ntral City Library students
sit along the walls to access the free Wi-Fi. Others are curled up in chairs, reading a
book that is crucial for their study. Walk a bit further along and there is a bank of
computers, with people waiting to access th em. They are there to access important
information, such as job seeking. The old da ys of advertisements in the paper are
diminishing, and now jobs are advertised on a range of intern et sites, including
Government sites such as the Work and Inco me job seek site. If someone finds a job,
more likely than not they will have to appl y online. It is almost impossible to do
anything these days without ac cess to the internet. Informa tion about, and access to,
Government services are increasingly available only through the web.
The public library is a place that is open to rich and poor alike. Our library services
should never be bound by someone’s ability to pay, but that principle is at risk in these
days of cost-cutting. Statistic s show that the introduction of  user charges results in
lower usage of public libraries, and this in  turn directly imp acts on our communities’
literacy outcomes. It adds to inequality by denying access to those who can least afford
to pay. The introduction of user charges in New Zealand in the past has resulted in
lower usage of public libraries. In A ugust 2009 Hamilton introduced a fee of $10 per
month for homebound customers, and the numbers using this service halved. A series of
charges introduced by the Rangitīkei District Council in the early 2000s resulted in a 35
percent decrease in borrowing. These charges—[ Interruption] Well, good question.
These charges were removed in 2005, resulti ng in a steady increase in issues. In 1999
Ashburton introduced a charge of $1 per issue for all adult books that were under 2
years old. In 1988 Napier introduc ed fees for selected fiction books and magazines, and
that resulted in a 65 percent drop in borrowing. In the Ashburton and Napier cases, after
a huge public opposition the councils subsequently reverted to a free issues policy, and
that resulted in an increase in issues.
Libraries are the holders of many precious collections. They are the storehouses of
history. I am thinking here of the important George Grey collections in the public
library in Auckland. Imagine these collections being developed and applied on a user-
pays basis. Do we really want unbalanced, profit-driven libraries that cater only for
immediate, popular choices rather than non- profitable alternatives ? The landscape in
which public libraries operated has changed significantly over the past few years. Rapid
technological change has seen the rise of  social networks, e-books, smartphones, and
many other mobile devices.
The scale of that change is impacting on public libraries worldwide, and countries
are responding to change and that pressure in different ways. Some, like Denmark, are
reinventing the library both physically and vi rtually into a vital national and community
asset, without which a community cannot think of itself as civilise d. In the UK, sadly,
some local authorities are responding to fi nancial pressure by closing libraries or
moving them to being run by community volunt eers, which has been a disastrous move.
However, other UK local authorities are reinvesting in libraries to ensure their
continued relevance and value. As Singapor e did 10 years ago, China is now investing
heavily in public library buildings and servic es to realise the economic and educational
benefits they offer communities.
Public libraries are vital community hubs. They connect people to their communities
and they contribute to New Zealand’s se nse of national identity. A well-informed,
educated population brings social and economic benefits to the whole country. Libraries
help provide this with e ducation, employment, and re creation opportunities. They
provide the means for anyone to interact with the Government, business, and each other,
regardless of means or income. With libraries now playing an important role in bridging
7 Nov 2012 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 6415
the digital divide for those w ithout personal computers or othe r devices, this bill will
also ensure that no one is charged for accessi ng the internet via libraries in accordance
with reasonable use requirements.
I am sure that all members in this Hous e will agree that li braries have a very
important place in our society. Voting for this bill will entrench in legislation the role of
free public library services for a ll citizens. It is a popular bill. It is a bill that surely we
can all agree with. In finishing, I want to quote that great feminist Germaine Greer, who
said: “A library is a place where you can lose your innocence without losing your
virginity.” But she also said: “Libraries are reservoirs of st rength, grace and wit,
reminders of order, calm, and continuity, lakes of mental energy, neither warm nor cold,
light nor dark … In any library in the wo rld, I am at home, unselfconscious, still and
absorbed.” So the question for the parties in this House is whether they support free
public library services being entrenched in New Zealand legislation. It is not a radical
idea. I urge parties to support this bill.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: This bill, the Local Government
(Public Libraries) Amendment Bill, is consti tutionally confused, it is fiscally flawed,
and it is awfully outdated. It actually says everything about how out of touch the Labour
Party is with the modern challenges for Ne w Zealand. It shows that the Labour Party is
living in the past. Yes, I accept that in the 1930s the local library was the pivotal access
point for people to get information. The reality today is that ultra-fast broadband and the
internet, in which this Government is inve sting $1.5 billion, is actually going to be far
more important for access to information this century.
The second thing is it is so nanny State.  You see, members opposite fundamentally
do not trust locally elected counc ils. What they want to do is  sit in their parliamentary
offices and tell elected councillors what they must make free.
The third thing about this bill is that it is fiscally reckless, like so many things that
Labour does. You know, Labour knows so well  how to spend othe r people’s money.
You see, everything that Labour members pride themselves on doing is coming to
Parliament and making some thing free. Well, I have got  news for members of the

items.speaker: Labour Party
items.text: somebody always pays. Whether it is the ratepayer or  the taxpayer, they
cannot pretend there is not a cost for somebody.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Oh, hang on—the Greens.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Well, we could take up the Greens. They say: “No, there
isn’t a cost. We just print money.”, but th is evening I am not going to go down that
road.
You see, the basic point is this: do members on this side of the House think libraries
are important? Of course we do. That is why we spent $70 million of public money on
the National Library—$70 million. If you look at  Vote Education, there was over $100
million spent by this Government on providing libraries in our schools for children.
It is absolutely proper that we in this Parliament have a say about how we spend
taxpayers’ money, but what this bill says is that we are going to overrule local councils
and say that they must spend money on public  libraries. They must make them free. I
could recite even in this Parliament speech  after speech after sp eech of local members
opposite saying that we must tr ust local democracy. So I si mply challenge the members
opposite—
Hon Damien O’Connor: What about the regional council in Canterbury, Nick?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: And I can hear Damien O’Connor poking his head up. Why
does he not trust the Grey District Council to  make the decision? Why does he not trust
the Westland District Council to make the decision? Why does he not trust the Buller
District Council to make this decision? Y ou see, members opposite cannot lecture this
Government about local democracy and then, wh en they come to thei r particular issue,
6416 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
say: “No, no, no. Those services must be free, regardless of what the local council might
decide.”
I also want to say how technologically illiterate this bill is. It again illustrates to this
Parliament how much Labour is living in the past and not the future. I would love the
next Labour member to explain this for me . Just down the road from the Nelson public
library—in fact, within 500 metr es—I have got three intern et cafes. They are little
businesses; they employ people. Their businesses have been affected by a directive from
the previous Labour Government that said th at there could not be any charge for the
public internet service, even for international visitors, and the consequence was a loss of
jobs for those businesses. So my challenge to members opposite—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: How many? Mr Little challenges how many. I reckon there
are about four or five people employed in each of those internet cafes. It is interesting—
why is it that those internet cafes were star ted by private enterprise ahead of the public
libraries? I will tell you why. Because private enterprise is innovative. It is able to move
with the times more quickly.
I ask members opposite what they have got against the provision of internet cafes,
Wi-Fi services, and those other things? For in stance, why is it that this bill would make
it illegal for my local library to charge a fee for a DVD? Do we really think it is such an
offence that a library servi ce, right alongside Video Ezy or  the local video store, can
also charge for a DVD? Do we really think Parliament has to pass a law banning a
council from putting any charge on a purely entertainment DVD? Have Labour
members become such a socialist society that  they wish that DVDs were free under the
great Labour Party vision that they have? I say not. I say this bill goes too far.
I also want to challenge the member’s assert ion that Unesco says that libraries have
to be free. What a load of hogwash! What a load of hogwash! I challenge the member to
tell us all those countries—whether it be the United States, whether it be the
Europeans—that have this sort of law on th eir books, that have respect for Unesco. The
Government’s own advice from officials is that  the member is flawed in her assertions
in that regard.
Our local public libraries right through Ne w Zealand have a very important service
and role to play. They provide a damned good service, which members on this side of
the House respect. Even when I was listeni ng to the member proposing this bill, she
struggled to find examples of a problem th at would justify this bill. I noticed she
remembered my colleague and the decision in Rangitīkei, which she then acknowledged
a council had been democratically elected to  change in 2005. So I say to the member
opposite, you are going to have to prove a lot better case for the wrong that you are
trying fix for Parliament to override the decision of councils.
This is a nanny State bill. This is a bill that is tied to books of the last century, rather
than the information age of th is century. This is a bill that says that members opposite
know better how to spend other people’s m oney than they do about how to create
wealth. This is a bill that speaks volumes a bout the lack of vision of the Labour Party
and how bereft it is of ideas for taking this country forward.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call the honourable
member Jacinda Ardern. As it is a 5-minute speech, I will ring the bell at 1 minute.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: What an absolute outrage to have that ex-Minister,
Nick Smith, stand up and tell this side of the House that a bill to try to preserve what
should be a sacred thing, and that is access to information via local libraries, is an
attempt to overrule councils, overrule local government, and gut th eir ability to self-
determination. I find it utterly outrageous to ha ve the former Minister, who has tried to
remove the four “well-beings” from local government’s mandate, can now stand up and
7 Nov 2012 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 6417
tell this House that our attempt to preser ve something that should be sacred is an
overriding of local government’s jurisdiction. Th at is a complete outrage, particularly
given that we have seen some examples in recent times of local government considering
paring back some of the services around lo cal libraries not because of choice but
because of pressure—the kind of pressure that that Government is happy to place on
local government, with no qualms whatsoever.
Bureaucracies are loading down local govern ment, and that means they are starting
to have to make choices between essential services and, for instance, having to send out
bureaucrats to individually, one by one, register tr ees, Mr Smith. That is the kind of
thing that that Government has decided is more of a priority than the kind of cost that
we would like to see maintained within councils, and that is the preservation of essential
services.
Nick Smith stood up and said this bill is constitutionally flawed. This bill is quite
simple. It is about maintaining what the publ ic would assume to be a natural right of
local constituents anyway. Most people w ould be astounded to th ink that we would
need to preserve in legislation free access to books and things like internet services. The
ex-Minister also said that the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband was going to solve all the
issues we have highlighted around access to th e internet. That is absolutely untrue. He
obviously has not heard of something called th e digital divide, and it is very real—so
much so that it is actually measured as one of the enforced lacks. Unicef uses it as a way
of demonstrating whether or not children ar e all getting the same start in life, by
whether they are able to access a computer a nd the internet. We know that that is an
issue in New Zealand—we know it. Material de privation, enforced lacks, has increased
under this Government, and now they think it is  fine to allow a situation where this will
get even worse, and will not even put in a fe w measures to protect the odd free service,
via, for instance, preserving what should be sacred.
In this party we recognise the important value of libraries—we always have. Norman
Kirk, a great Labour Prime Minister, left sc hool at 13. He educated himself via a local
library. That side of the House may try to call those services antiquated. They are very
much still the hub of our comm unities. I know that where I reside we have seen those
services under threat even in recent times. Grey Lynn Library, which was voted by users
across central Auckland as the best librar y we have, was recently threatened with
closure, as the council came under increasing pressure to cut services.
The natural place that they go? Those qui et achievers; they look to our quiet
achievers and they threaten them, and yet those are the places th at our parents go, for
playgroups and to take their ch ildren for story reading. It is where our job seekers go
when they want to access a serv ice that is a little more safe  and secure than a Work and
Income kiosk. It is where our students and our elderly go. [Interruption] If they are safe,
why is it then that there was debate, Sim on Bridges, in Tauranga about charging for
general hireage? You would have to rent a book for $2 a go. We are not even talking
about the best renters, like Fifty Shades of Grey, Simon—I know you would be an avid
reader. We are talking about the general checking out of books at $2 a go. If that side of
the House thinks that is acceptable, then fine , vote against this bill, but on this side of
the House we want to preserve our libraries and that is why we are in full support.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: You can only imagine yourself, or oneself,
in the Labour Party strategy room, and they are thinking—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Scary.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, yes, but in this instance we are going to go there and we are
going to think “OK, we’re going to oppose the commissioners coming in to do a good
job and pick up after Environment Canterbury because we really want local
democracy.” Then they move on to the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority post
6418 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
the earthquake and they say “It is really not fair of that bad National Government to take
away local democracy.” Then you move forward a month or two and you go to the
Local Government and Environment Comm ittee and hear the submissions from
councils, fully backed up by their mates in  Labour, and they say “Taking away self-
determination from local democracy—bad old National Government.” Then we have in
front of us a bill, the Local Government (P ublic Libraries) Amendment Bill, that does
exactly that. So what does Labour want ? Well, I do not think Labour knows what it
wants.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: A new leader.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Well, yes, Labour wants a new l eader, and it cannot even make up
its mind about that. It is tearing itself apar t as we speak. But we are now dealing with
this bill in the name of Darien Fenton, and a ll she is doing in this bill is shifting the
costs. All those fine words a bout access to learning and acce ss to libraries are all very
well, and crossing the digital divide and finding jobs is fantastic,  and finding shelter
from the cold weather, which is what they do in my part of the country, is all very well,
but who is going to pay for it? Well, under Da rien Fenton’s “Labour-lite” world, it is all
going to be for free. Who is going to pay for it? Well, not the ratepayers.
So here we go. Let us have a look at the pur pose of this bill. Clause 4 states: “The
purpose of this Act is to amend the Local Government Act … to expand the public
library services that local authorities are required to provide for free.” So if it is going to
be for free, who is going to pay for it? Le t us just hold that thought for a minute,
because we will move on to clause 5: “Section 142 replaced”—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Jacqui, it’s called taxes. Hello, Jacqui.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Oh, it is the taxpayers! The memb er from the other side of the
House has now decided that the taxpayer is going to pay for local library services. Well,
let us ring up Local Government New Zeala nd and tell it that its Labour mates are now
in favour of a complete takeover of local  government by central government, and that
the taxpayer is now going to pick up the tab fo r library services. Let us just remember
that thought.
Let us go into new section 142(1)(a), which st ates: “the residents in the district or
region of the local authority are entitled to join the library free of charge;”. Well, hello,
here is some news, Darien Fenton: they can  do that already. It is already in existing
legislation. So let us go to (b) and have anot her crack: “the library shall not charge any
resident of the authority’s district or re gion for the use of library material, including
books, non-print resources, and digital informa tion;”. Well, who is going to pay? Who
is going to pay for these services? Is it going to be free? Is it going to be the taxpayer, as
Phil Twyford is no doubt going to represent? Who is going to pay? Who is going to pay
for these services if they are going to be for free?
I just want to make one final point on this  bill, and I go to new section 142(2): “The
National Librarian must present an annual re port to Parliament on the implementation
by local authorities of subsection (1), …”. Is  that not fantastic? The National Librarian
is now going to become the library police for the Labour Party. So, not content with
drawing money out of thin air—no, should I say printing money, because I suspect that
is the only way they are going to be able to afford this policy—or printing money to
give effect to this bill, it is also going to make the National Librarian the library police
for Labour so that it can go and check on local government. Here we have Darien
Fenton, and all this member is doing is shifting the cost. She cuts across all principles of
funding of local government. This member s hould be ashamed of the ignorance she is
bringing to this House. I do not support this bill.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I am pleased to speak on behalf
of my colleague Gareth Hughes, who is the Green Party’s lib rary and archives
7 Nov 2012 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 6419
spokesperson, on this, the Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill. The
Green Party will be supporting this bill in the name of Darien Fenton, because we
believe that everybody has the right to info rmation, and because, in an increasingly
unequal society due to the economic policies of  this Government, libraries are a place
where everybody can have free access to info rmation. This bill is not telling local
councils how they should run their libraries; it  is just enshrining th at free right to read,
and to access books, digital info rmation, and the other servi ces that libraries provide.
We value libraries because they are the storehouses of knowledge. They play a vital role
in our communities and in the functioning of this Parliament in providing access to
information and providing in our communities a gathering place.
In Christchurch, where we have not been  able to access the library in Worcester
Street post-quake, it was a major cause for celebration when the new library opened
opposite the old Christchurch Convention Centre in the old Vbase building. It is open, it
is clean, and it is a place where children, mi grants, and older citizens go because they
can access books for free. This is why we support this bill. I would like to quote
something that Carl Sagan said about libraries: “The library connects us with the insight
and knowledge, painfully extracted from Nature , of the greatest minds that ever were,
with the best teachers, drawn from the entire planet and fr om all of our history, to
instruct us without tiring, a nd to inspire us to make our own contribution to the
collective knowledge of the hum an species. I think the heal th of our civilization, the
depth of our awareness about the underpinni ngs of our culture and our concern for the
future can all be tested by how well we support our libraries.”
Under the current Local Government Act, local authorities that provide a library need
to ensure only that local residents can join it free of charge. T hose councils do not have
to enshrine a right of free access. We have seen the growth of membership charges,
whether it is by rental for books or through other charges, and that goes against the
whole Kiwi culture. Kiwis love our libraries.  In 2003 a survey of cultural activities and
spending found that visiting libraries was the third most popular activity—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: They love barbecues too; you’re not making them free.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: Mr Bridges, 39 percent of the population visited in a 4-week
period. Around half of all New Zealanders ar e members of our libraries, and in some
places membership is at 80 percent of th e local population. Another survey in 2009 by
Kiwis Count found that 82 percent of people were happy with the services provided by
their library—the happiest out of any council service. That is because New Zealanders
value free access to books and library services. Where councils have attempted to put in
place charges there has often been a str ong resistance from the community, and in
places like Tauranga the council has had to retreat and not institute those book charges.
And where those councils—like Ashburton, as Darien Fenton mentioned—have put in
place charges, what has happened? Patronage of the library has declined. Where you put
in place those user charges, who pays? Who bears the brunt of t hose measures? It is
people who can least afford to pay: migr ants, people on a benefit, people on low
incomes, the people who would get the most  out of free access to  the libraries and
getting access to books.
This bill is a very useful one because it means that libraries have to ensure that books
and the knowledge they provide is free. It is also a way, as  others have alluded to, of
bridging the digital divide, because not ev erybody has a computer  at home, and by
having free access to digital servic es, we can get over that barrier . So it is a bill that we
will be supporting because it is consistent with what done elsewhere internationally by
not charging for books.

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak on the
Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill. I want to start off by
6420 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 7 Nov 2012
acknowledging the great job that so many libra rians do around our country. I also want
to start by acknowledging that in this Parlia ment we currently have a parliamentary
inquiry into 21 st century learning environments. I am  not going to go into the detail of
that inquiry except to say that I do not suppor t this bill, because I think there are rapid
changes happening in terms of technology a nd information management, and that what
this bill does—although I acknowledge Darien Fenton, the member who has put this bill
to the House—is misguided. I think it is mi sguided for a number of reasons and I want
to talk through them today.
The first thing that I would like to say is that when we look across th e country in
terms of information management, when we look across the country in terms of libraries
in Grey Lynn versus libraries in North Shore,  there is a difference in practice, so to
provide a statute that puts things in place,  particularly, even, terms around charging for
digital information and books, will in my view  legislate what may be outdated terms in
a period of time. That is the first point I want to make.
The second point that I want  to make, and it has already been made by a number of
my colleagues, is that to put these costs on local governme nt and to say that every
public library is going to be free is a very dramatic change and it is contrary to a number
of other speeches that we ha ve heard in this House. I wa nt to touch on something that
Eugenie Sage has already said. Yes, ther e is an issue generally around access to
information, but that involves a range of policies, the term “library” itself, the role of the
libraries in the future, the role of libraries with regard to both public libraries and school
libraries, and the role of libraries in terms of broadband policy—these are all things that
we have been considering as part of the se lect committee inquiry. But to prescribe those
terms and to prescribe policies, and to prescribe certain information management in
legislation and say that every single local authority in the country will have free access
around that, in my view, is a flawed piece of legislation.
I do want to say a couple of other things. Another thing I want to  point out is that it
is not just about the terms that are in the b ill; there has also been an issue raised around
UNESCO and its obligations under UNESCO. I do want to make  the point that actually
when you look in more detail at  those guidelines, the guidelin es are in principle and I
would think there is a very valid reason fo r that. That is that right around the world
many countries are acknowledging that whether it is through th e greater role that some
school libraries are playing, or whether it is through more  online learning, there are
rapid changes in information management. My caution to this Parliament is that
although this bill may have been well intentioned by Darien Fenton, I cannot support
this bill, because I think that what is  needed—and I know that we have got a
parliamentary select committee looking at some of these issues—is a much more
holistic approach to information manageme nt and the access to information. In my
view, I cannot support this bill for that reason.
The other main point that I want to ma ke is that Opposition members stand up and
say to other members across this House that in some way we do not support information
management and access to information, when we are putting $1.5 billion—that is one of
the greatest enablers in this  country—into ultra-fast broa dband. That is one of the
greatest enablers particularly for disadvant aged communities. Many members in this
House have heard of projects like Manaiaka lani, where we are seeing a huge uptake by
Māori and Pacific kids. I am very proud of some  of the policies th at we are putting in
place to enable disadvantaged communities to have access to information. This bill is
flawed. It may be well intentioned, but it is flawed and it does not take into account the
rapid changing nature of both technology and information management in the world.
Thank you.
7 Nov 2012 Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill 6421

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First on
the Local Government (Public Libraries) Amendment Bill. This is a very interesting bill
because the public libraries of this country are institutions in their own right. We all
know of some of the great public librarie s located around New Zealand, and we have
grown up with those public libraries in our to wns, in our villages, in our cities, and in
our districts. They very much are the cen tre of many communities. As the explanatory
note of this bill does say at the beginning: “Public libraries play an important role in our
communities by helping New Zealanders to achieve access to information and
entertainment. They also provide important  community hubs.” That is very much the
case. At this point in time, New Zealand Fi rst will be supporting this bill because we
feel that it does require scrutiny and it does need to go through to the Local Government
and Environment Committee.
We are very concerned about what is happeni ng in local governme nt in terms of the
four social well-beings being taken away by this Government—in terms of the social,
cultural, economic, and envir onmental well-beings. Therefore,  if this Government is
going to focus local authorities simply on ra tes, rubbish, and sewerage, and take away
many of the social and cultural responsibilit ies, then perhaps our libraries could be
threatened in the future. That is not to sa y that they would be immediately, but they
could be threatened in the future. That would be a sad day for many communities in
New Zealand.
I can recall an instance that we had on the North Shore where our Birkenhead
Library unfortunately got demolished before there was a building and resource consent
to replace it, due to some error in the bureau cratic system. Unfortunately, the lovely old

LAND TRANSPORT (ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENTIAL BREATH TESTS)
First Reading

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I move, That the Land Transport
(Admissibility of Evidential Breath Test s) Amendment Bill be  now read a first time.  I
nominate the Transport and Industrial Relati ons Committee to consider the bill. When
this House first passed into law the Land Transport Act back in  1998 it established a
strict and prescriptive regime around the evidential breath test and blood testing of
drivers suspected of driving while under the influence.
The legislation has been intensively scruti nised by the courts over the years. Those
charged with excess blood-alcohol levels of ten engage lawyers to test, probe, and
nullify the technical aspects of the law in at tempting to avoid conviction. The case law
around this area is extensive. It is complicat ed, and it provides, in my opinion, far too
7 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6427
many opportunities for escape from conviction resulting from what most ordinary Kiwis
would call legal loopholes. I am delighted, therefore, that th e Minister of Police, the
Hon Anne Tolley, has recently ordered that  the Police should come up with a better
system for testing drunk drivers, because there are too many escape routes. I applaud
that review, and I will look forward to the outcome of it in due course.
Today there are still too many people escapi ng prosecution, and it is the closing off
of one of those escape loopholes that my bill seeks to address. My Land Transport
(Admissibility of Evidential Breath Test s) Amendment Bill will remedy a small but
significant oversight, one not contemplated by the House when it passed the principal
Act back in 1998. My bill amends the Land Transport Act to broaden the circumstances
where a positive evidential breath test is admissible evidence in seeking a prosecution
under the Act.
Under section 77 of the present law a positive breath test is not admissible in
evidence if the suspect has el ected to have a blood test subsequent to having blown a
positive evidential breath test. Section 70A confers the right of an accused drink-driver,
having produced that positive evidential breath test, to request that a blood test be taken.
The accused driver has 10 minutes in which to  make that decision. However, the law is
very specific, and once a decision is made to  elect to have a blood test taken, at that
moment the preceding evidential breath test is  no longer able to be used in evidence in
any subsequent court case. That is section 77( 3)(b). Under the law, the test is statute
barred.
The principal Act assumes that once the option to elect a blood sample has been
exercised by the accused drink-driver, blood will in fact be available to be taken from
the accused drink-driver. The principal Act simply does not contemplate a situation
where the particular medical or personal phys ical characteristics of the accused mean
that a blood sample may not be able to be drawn from that person.
The Act is actually silent on what is to happen when a blood test is elected but a
sample cannot be collected because a medical officer is unable to obtain a sample. But
the Act does make it clear th at once a blood test has been  nominated, the previous
evidential test is no longer admissible. The original intent of the legislation obviously
was to provide statutory clarity that, once obtained, the blood test should have evidential
precedence over the earlier breath test. So let us consider when it may be, for instance,
and under what possible circumstances it w ould be, that a blood sample perhaps may
not be available from an accused drink-driver.
A recent Rotorua District Court case, the Police v Childs , heard before Judge M A
MacKenzie in just July of th is year, provides an absolutely excellent example of the
situation my bill seeks to remedy. There the defendant, Childs, who was positive for
hepatitis C and also an intravenous drug user of many years, was apprehended by police
and underwent a breath-screening test that returned a result of 400 micrograms. He then
underwent an evidential breath test that re turned an even incr eased result of 655
micrograms. He was then advised of his ri ght to a blood test, and, of course, he
immediately accepted it. As the tourniquet wa s applied, Mr Childs taunted the medical
officer by saying “Good luck” and smiling. Three attempts later, made over 40 minutes,
the medical officer was simply not able to locate an appropriate vein and no adequate
blood sample was obtained from Mr Childs. Years of intravenous drug use had more
than taken its toll on the veins in his arms.
Judge MacKenzie examined in detail existing case law around this area. I commend
members to take the time to read her very good judgment, which sets out in clear detail
why my bill is required to remedy the s ituation where, following two positive breath
tests, Her Honour was forced to, by statute, dismiss the drink-driving charges against
Childs. Childs literally got off scot-free.
6428 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 7 Nov 2012
The judge said, and I quote directly from th e judgment: “It is ac cepted that there is
no specific statutory provision which addresses the situation where a blood sample is
not in fact collected on the basis that the medical officer or practitioner has been unable
to obtain a sample such as in Mr Childs’ cas e. I am acutely conscious of the need and
importance of accountability for drink-drivers. The frustrati on in this case”, said the
judge, “is that Mr Childs cl early contravened the sprit of  the legislation given the
evidential breath test result, an d in that sense is evading re sponsibility for his actions of
drink-driving and the conseque nces of it.” The judge went  on to say: “A statutory
amendment would be required to address the unusual circumstances such as Mr Childs’,
where blood cannot be taken for medical reasons.” This bill provides that statutory
amendment.
I was pleased to hear from Mike Noon on behalf of the Automobile Association say
that the Automobile Association supports the in tent of this bill. It will be suggesting to
the select committee that the words “any reason” be narrowed slightly to identify that
the reason should be of a medi cal nature. Doing so would, of course, prevent a situation
where, for instance, no testing equipment or no testing officer was available, thus
preventing a blood sample from being taken.  That is a matter very appropriate for
consideration by the select committee, and it is a suggestion I am more than happy to
explore. I certainly appreciate the support of the Automobile Association.
I note that the Attorney-General has tabled  a report on my bill under section 7 of the
New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. The nub of the report from his officials is that my bill
would in some way infringe upon the rights of a person to be presumed innocent until
proven guilty. Nothing could be further from my intention in moving this bill. The
purpose of this bill is to en tirely confirm the previously very clear intention of this
House that driving under th e influence of alcohol is both legally and socially
unacceptable, and those who do should, afte r evidence beyond reasonable doubt has
been established in a court of law, be held accountable for their actions and accept the
full legal consequences of those actions.
My bill does not remove the presumption of innocence. It merely provides that
should blood not be available fo r testing, then the police shall be permitted to introduce
into evidence before a court of law the evidential breath test taken prior to the
nomination of a blood test. It would absolutely, of course, still be up to the police
prosecutors to prove their case to the sa tisfaction of beyond reasonable doubt. That is
the measure of all criminal convictions w ithin our judicial sy stem. I respectfully
disagree with the views expr essed by the Attorney-General’s officials. In so doing, I
remind honourable members that it is Parliament, this Chamber itself, that is master of
its own legislative-making capacity.
So, in conclusion, this bill seeks to re medy a loophole not anticipated when the
principal legislation was enacted. It is an amendment that will impact on people such as
Mr Childs, who do not and cannot currently accept responsibility for the consequences
of their drink-driving, due to an omission a nd an oversight on behalf of this House in
the principal Act.
I would like to acknowledge and thank my colleague the senior  Government whip,
Michael Woodhouse, for his help, support, and guidance with this bill. The genesis of
this bill was his, and arose from a previous court decision where similar circumstances
to the Childs case prevailed. I look forward to the select committee consideration of the
bill and to progressing the bill through the House. I thank honourable members for its
favourable consideration.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Let me say at the outset
that we in the Labour Party seek to be a constructive Opposition and to work with the
Government where we can on legislation, so  we will support this legislation, the Land
7 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6429
Transport (Admissibility of Evidential Br eath Tests) Amendment Bill, going to the

view of the Automobile Association that the bill as it is worded currently is too broad,
and we would also want to see some amendm ent to those final words in the bill, “for

forward to the debate and the consideration at the select committee.
Clearly, it does seem inadequate that where an evidential breath test finds or suggests
that someone is over the drink-driving limit,  there appears to be a mechanism by which
a small number of people may be able to avoi d prosecution. It is important to reinforce,
I think, that we are dealing with probably a very small number of people—in fact, I

really is a significant issue th at is so desperately in need  of attention. In fact, the
member suggested that there are many ways  to avoid prosecution for a charge of
drinking in excess of the limit. If that were  the case, then surely this should be a
Government bill that addressed all of thos e issues. We wonder on this side just how

I have to look at some of the language that  Mr Simpson has used around this issue.
He cited the case of a defendant who was a pparently hepatitis C positive. I do not know

that fact into the debate at all. That pers on was also an intravenous drug user. I read in
the newspaper Mr Simpson referring to th is as an issue that was pretty much
specifically designed to capture people who ar e intravenous drug user s. In fact, he has
not offered any other reason why it might be  difficult to take blood from someone.
There are a range of reasons why it may be difficult to  take blood from somebody. One
is being overweight, another is stress. At a time of stress, the body actually withdraws
the blood from the limbs—the arms, the legs —back towards the vital organs and the
brain. It is the fight or flight  response. It is quite a norma l thing to happen and, indeed,
if someone were found to be dr iving over the limit, it is probably fair to say that that
would be a stressful situation and that fight or flight mechanism may kick in and it may
be difficult to draw blood from these people.  But these situations have not come up in
Mr Simpson’s discussion at all. He has focu sed this solely on a group of people whom I
suspect he deems to be less worthy of a reasonable hearing before the law. Because they
are intravenous drug users, he has decided that they are somehow less worthy before the
law.
You have to wonder exactly wh at it is that is driving Mr Simpson here, or why he
has used that language. Maybe he is trying to convince the good National voting people
out there that this will not affect them some how, because this is directed at a very
narrow group of people and not at them. I do not know. Mr Simpson might be able to
enlighten us as to why he has used the particul ar language that he has, but that is up to
him. Suffice it to say that there are a numbe r of reasons why it might be impossible to
draw blood.
I do want to say, though, that we must be mindful of the Attorney-General’s report.
Mr Simpson referred to it as the Attorney-General’s officials’ report. I think that is
unfair on the Attorney-General. The Attorney-G eneral’s signature is  on this. I know
John Banks has set a new standard for si gning documents and wh ether or not you are
supposed to have read them before you sign them, but I take the Attorney-General’s
signature on there as this being something th at he has not only read but something that
he supports. So this is the Attorney-General’s report, and we do have to be mindful of it.
In fact, if the Attorney-General were to o ffer his thoughts in this debate, that would be
6430 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 7 Nov 2012
welcome on this side of the House. But we do need to be mindful of what the Attorney-
General said.
I find it ironic that this Land Transport (A dmissibility of Evidential Breath Tests)
Amendment Bill is being promoted by a National Party member. It is being supported
by the National Party, and it will get, I am su re, the support of th e governing parties
tonight as well as some of the Opposition part ies, when it will have such a small impact
on the road toll and the harm  caused by drink driving, when  in the same breath those
parties will refuse to support lowering the drink-drive limit from 0.08 to 0.05. That is a
measure we know is evidence-based and will ha ve a significant imp act on the harm on
the roads caused by alcohol. The Ministry of Transport has provided evidence to the
Minister of Transport that it will reduce th e number of people killed on our roads every
year by up to 30. Up to 30 lives can be save d every year if the G overnment would just
accept the advice of its own officials and would follow public opinion. Eighty-five
percent of New Zealanders support loweri ng the drink-drive limit from 0.08 to 0.05,
which international evidence tells us not only has an impact on the people who drive
with a blood-alcohol limit of between 0.05 and 0.08 but also significantly reduces the
number of people who are h eavily intoxicated who get behind the wheel, drive their
vehicle, cause accidents, and kill people.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: How?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I heard the word “How?” fr om the far side there. The
evidence is actually quite cl ear and quite simple. It is  quite simple. A limit of 0.05
requires people to make a decision about whether or not they get behind the wheel much
earlier in the proces s of consuming alcohol, because  once they get over 0.05 but are
below 0.08 they lose the capacity to make a se nsible decision about whether or not they
should get behind the wheel. It is as simp le as that. The evidence supports it. The
evidence that the Minister was given supports it. Public opinion supports it. It is what
people want. It is the right th ing to do. It will save lives, and yet this Government will
not do it. What it is doing instead is a piecemeal  piece of legislation like this, which is
fine in and of itself, but it is meaningless in the grand scheme of trying to reduce the
road toll and trying to reduce the harm caused by alcohol and the harm caused by drink-
driving. It is, in fact, from the language used by Mr Simpson, being used to isolate some
members of our community and further di vide our community, which we know this
National Party is so very, very good at doing.
So although we appreciate that there is probably some positive motivation behind
what Mr Simpson is trying to do, and although we appreciate that there is an inadequacy
in the law, which we will work with the Government to tidy up, we think there are much
larger issues that need to be addre ssed, and could be being addressed, by this
Government if it was actually prepared to  do the right thing and address the harm
caused by alcohol on our roads with a piece of  legislation that would actually make
some difference.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: It is great to follow
King’s College old boy Iain Lees-Gallo way, who is now, we know, a social
campaigner. It is great to see someone s ticking up so staunchl y for intravenous drug
users, a group that has not been stuck for before. That is one interpretation. The other
interpretation is that that pa rty is so low in the polls that  those members are looking for
any interest group to support them. That is pr obably the interpreta tion that I would go
with.
No one is saying, Mr Lees-Galloway, that this  is the biggest issue that has ever come
before this House. No one is saying that. The member Scott Simpson himself should be
commended for finding this issue—it is a discre te issue, it is a narrow issue, but in its
way it is an issue that should be remedied, and there is a problem here. We understand
7 Nov 2012 Land Transport (Evidential Breath Tests) Amdt Bill 6431
that the evidential breath-tes ting happens, then there is a 10-minute rights period, and
then we go to the blood test . I have no experience of that test; some members in this
House may do, but I have none. But there is a real problem here. There is a real
problem. We understand that some 10 years ag o the law reinstated the right for blood
tests for all drivers, and to compensate fo r that, and for the rem oval of the right of
drivers to challenge the accuracy of the evid ential breath test, we have got the problem
here that has arisen and that the member  Scott Simpson has brought to this House,
because case law has made it clear that it needs to.
This bill aims to close a l oophole whereby a small, select  group of drunk drivers are
able to avoid prosecution. The truth is, Mr  Lees-Galloway, it is a small number of
people. It will basically be just intravenous drug users, where they cannot have blood
taken from them because the vein cannot be drawn from.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: That’s one reason. What about the other reasons?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: There may be other reasons fo r it, as well, but that will
absolutely be the issue that is coming befo re the courts, and th e case law tends to
indicate that. So if a pers on complies with the blood-taking process and they cannot be
prosecuted—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. Honourable members, the time has come for me to leave the Chair.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

7 Nov 2012 Business of the House 6345 
WEDNESDAY, 7 NOVEMBER 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE 
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Leader of the House) : Following discussions in the 
Business Committee yesterday, I seek leave for Wednesday, 14 November 2012 to be a 
members’ day, despite Standing Order 74(1), and for any bills drawn from the ballot on 
Thursday, 8 November to be set down fo r first reading on Wednesday, 14 November, 
despite Standing Order 281(2). 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Economy and Government Financial Position—Reports 
1. Hon TAU HENARE (National) to the Minister of Finance: What reports has he 
received on the Government’s financial position? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Crown’s financial statements for 
the 3 months to 30 September were issued t oday. They confirm that the Government is 
keeping its spending under cont rol, but that revenue can be  affected by the uncertain 
global economic situation and its impact on New Zealand. For example, in the first 3 
months of this fiscal year Crown tax re venue was $295 million below forecast and core 
Crown interest revenue was $147 million lower than expected. This was partially offset 
by Crown expenses being $200 million below fo recast, including slightly lower than 
forecast welfare expenses. The operating deficit before gains and losses was $2 billion 
for the 3-month period. 
Hon Tau Henare: What approach is the Government taking to ensure it continues to 
carefully manage its finances so it does return to surplus? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government’s target is to return to surplus by 2014-15 
so that we will then have choices about repaying debt, resuming contributions to the 
New Zealand Superannuation Fund, or targe ting more investment in priority public 
services. To achieve this we will need to keep on top of the factors we can control, such 
as remaining prudent with any new spending and borrowing. We will also continue to 
focus very strongly on delivering more public services, even where there is less money, 
to ensure that we s upport those who need ou r services. This is important in a world 
where economic conditions are unpredictable and could have unpredictable impacts on 
New Zealand Government revenue. 
Hon Tau Henare : What reports has he received  on the global ec onomic situation 
and its likely impact on New Zealand and Government finances? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Earlier this week Treas ury published its monthly Economic 
Indicators for November, focusing on global growt h. It notes that more than 5 years 
after the onset of the financial crisis th e world economy is performing again below 
expectation. World economic growth in the first half of 2012 wa s generally below IMF 
forecasts, and the latest forecast for world out put, issued last month, contained further 
downward revisions. If global growth does remain weaker than expected, it would affect 
New Zealand’s growth and Government finances. 
6346 Questions for Oral Answer 7 Nov 2012 
Hon Tau Henare: How is New Zealand’s economy performing compared with most 
other developed economies, and what policy pr escription would put this performance at 
risk? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: We continue to perform at m oderate levels, but nevertheless 
better than most other develope d countries. In the first half  of this year New Zealand 
grew by 1.6 percent, which is higher than growth rates in the US, Japan, Canada, the 
UK, and the euro area over the same period. Our quarterly growth rate is about the same 
as Australia’s. Policies that would put th is at risk would include borrowing more, 
spending more, and printing money, which would fuel costs for households and 
businesses and put jobs at risk.  
Hon David Parker: How can the Minister stand in this House and pretend that it is 
good news that the Government deficit of $2.1 billion is $490 million—or 27 percent—
higher than he projected in his Budget just months ago? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I am not saying it is good news; I am just saying it is the 
news. It is the news and it is  a snapshot in a long journey towards repairing the damage 
that the previous Labour Government did to the economy and to Government finances. 
Hon David Parker: Is it correct that in addition to an increasing Government deficit, 
the New Zealand economy is running the se cond-worst current account deficit in the 
developed world this year, and is projec ted by the IMF to have the worst current 
account deficit in the developed world next ye ar; if it is correct, doe s he agree with the 
Governor of the Reserve Bank, Mr Wheeler, that that is far too high? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: On the first issue, of course we want to see the Government 
deficit coming back. It was $18 billion 2 y ears ago, it was $9 billion last year, and we 
are on the track towards about $7 billion for this year and a $2 billion deficit the 
following year. Quarterly figures  are not pushing us off that  track. In respect of the 
current account deficit, I would take more no tice of what the member said if it had not 
been the case that under his Government it doubled from 4 percent to 8 percent, which 
were the worst levels New Zealand has ever had. That was from the party that is now 
preaching the loudest about fixing it. 
Schools, Canterbury—Proposed Closures and Mergers and Confidence in Minister 
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
have confidence in all his Ministers; if so, why? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes; because they are working harder for a 
brighter future for all New Zealanders. 
David Shearer : Does he have confidence in hi s Minister of Education and her 
management of the future of education in Christchurch; if so, why? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Yes; because she is committing $1 billion to new schooling in 
Christchurch. I think what we all need to understand in respect  of Christchurch is that a 
major earthquake took place that has changed the patterns of where people live. But it 
has also presented an opportunity to deliver 21 st century schools to Christchurch. I 
simply make this point: we are not rebu ilding the central business district in 
Christchurch with exactly the same buildi ngs; we are using the opportunity to deliver 
arguably the most liveable city in New Zeal and, and then maybe, just maybe, there will 
be an opportunity to deliver better schooling facilities for yo ungsters in Christchurch. I 
think that is a good thing. 
David Shearer : Does he stand by his undertaki ng that he will personally look 
through the response from each Christchurch school; if so, why does he think it is 
necessary for a Prime Minister to personally review submissions from all these schools 
if he does in fact have confidence in his Minister? 
7 Nov 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 6347 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Yes, and I would point out that  the Minister is personally 
visiting all of the schools. I understand that 35 of the 37 schools have  agreed to that. 
Why am I personally doing that? Well, I take a personal interest in Christchurch. It is 
one of the Government’s four key priorities , and I gave that commitment to the people 
of Christchurch because they kept on read ing nonsense from Chris Hipkins that was 
getting printed in the Press. 
David Shearer: Why will his Government not tell the communities affected by the 
closure and merger proposals what all the options identified by the ministry are? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The purpose now is, with those affected schools, to go through 
all of the options for those clusters, to ta lk about what the optio ns might be and the 
reasons why, and to potenti ally come up with some good solutions. What the 
Government is saying to the people of Christ church, to those parents who are affected, 
and to those schools, is that  we are listening to you, but we  are also listening to the 
advice we are receiving about what is changi ng. We are going to spend a billion dollars 
over the next 10 years— 
David Shearer: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I have been listening for quite a 
while. I actually asked why he will not tell us what the options are that were put forward 
by the Ministry of Education. 
Mr SPEAKER: The member is welcome to repeat his question. 
David Shearer : Why will his Government not tell the communities affected by 
closure and merger proposals what all the options identified by the ministry are?

It is very difficult to sustain a manufactured  crisis in the face of economic facts like

looking at massive cuts in welfare and h ealth services, and 500,000 jobs in the UK 
public sector to be slashed in the next 4 years, that is a re al crisis, not the phoney crisis 
that the Opposition is trying to paper over. 
METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green) : Later tonight my bill to almost halve 
child poverty, the Income Ta x (Universalisation of In-work Tax Credit) Amendment 
Bill, will have its vote in the House. I wa nt to thank all those community organisations, 
Every Child Counts, the Child Poverty Action Group, Champions for Children, and 
many other groups and individuals who ha ve written and emailed, tweeted and 
facebooked, marched, rallied, and otherwise worked to have this bill pass its first 
reading tonight.  
It is with genuine sorrow that I report th at we are still yet to find the one more vote 
we need to send this bill to the Social Se rvices Committee. All those parties supporting 
the bill tonight have been given a pair of infant socks—baby socks—as a small gesture 
from me to acknowledge their commitment to finding a real solution to the poverty that 
6366 General Debate 7 Nov 2012 
is suffered by a quarter of a million children in New Zealand today. I have one pair of 
baby socks left, because we need only one vote from one party to pass the bill. That one 
vote will bring the family income of an  estimated 100,000 New Zealand children above 
the poverty line. That one vote will ensure th at these children have a warm, dry home, 
shoes on their feet, and food in their bellies.  
Many organisations have expressed their distress at Peter Dunne’s decision to oppose 
my bill. During the 2011 election he signed a pledge with a group called Closer 
Together Whakatata Mai. That pledge sa ys: “As a politician, I choose to commit to

I have offered Peter Dunne and the Nati onal Government two compromises on my

moment, if you work and you receive a benef it, superannuation, or a student allowance,

hard-working efforts of low-income families,  but he has refused to recognise the hard-
working efforts of this group of low-in come families—some 40,000 DPB recipients 
who work, and another 20,000 who will be expect ed to work at least 15 hours a week 
next year. They all go unrecognised by Peter Dunne.  
I have also offered an amendment to th e Government and Peter Dunne that would 
allow a family to retain the in-work tax credit for 6 months after they lose a job or have

New Zealanders every year, or a natural disast er, as we have seen in this country, the 
personal and financial strain for those hard-working families is enormous. One vote is 
all that those families need.  
But I must confess that these compromises I offered to Peter Dunne to meet his—
what I consider to be somewhat irrational —needs were hard to stomach in the offering, 
because the Green Party believes that hard-working families are also those who care for 
their kids, whether in paid work or not . Hard-working parents are those who are 
deserving of dignity and decent treatment b ecause they care for their kids. One vote is 
all that these families need. One vote is all that their children need. Thank you.

gave authority for the transfer of part of the bed of the Tauranga Moana, the Tauranga 
Harbour, to what was then the Mount Ma unganui Borough Council,  and what is now 
the Tauranga City Council, for its sewerage scheme and other municipal purposes.  
The improvements in sewage treatment and discharge in Aotearoa New Zealand over 
the last 100 years are due in no small measure to iwi such as Ng ā Pōtiki and many 
others who have championed clean water and th e health of our harbours, our rivers, and 
our inshore coast, and sought to safeguard th ese areas from the indifference of local 
authorities. As the Waitangi Tribunal said in  its report on the Tauranga Moana claim: 
“for decades, local councils regarded Tauranga Harbour as the obvious repository for 
sewage.” It was as late as the 1950s, at  Mount Maunganui, that the sewerage system 
was still very primitive. Sewage effluent there could end up in an open drain. Residents 
relied on septic tanks right th rough until the 1970s, with the a ssociated risk of effluent 
leakage into the harbour and waterways. So it was this reclama tion within the south-
eastern arm of Tauranga Harbour, the Rangataua  estuary, that the principal Act and this 
bill deal with. That was in response to the inadequacies of a growing population relying 
on septic tanks. So in 1972 the borough coun cil’s scheme involved this reclamation 
within the estuary and the construction of oxidation ponds, and effluent was proposed to 
be discharged directly into the estuary, until an ocean outfall was built at Omanu.  
It was Tauranga Māori, including the kaumātua of Ngā Pōtiki, who strongly opposed 
this reclamation and the oxidation ponds b ecause of their effects on the estuary, the 
destruction of a flourishing ecosystem on the tidal flats, and their whole desire to protect 
their ancestral landscape, their taonga of the harbour, and to protect their shellfish beds. 
When you read through the Waitangi Tribunal report and its descript ion of the intense 
efforts that Ng ā Pōtiki made to try to protect the hea lth of this landscape, it is very 
7 Nov 2012  Mt Maunganui Reclamation & Empowering Act Repeal Bill 6381 
interesting to compare those efforts with the efforts of iwi now to protect the health of 
our beloved awa and roto, our rivers and lakes. Back in 1972 Tauranga Māori convinced 
the Pollution Advisory Council of the time to reclassify the harbour waters to a standard 
that would prevent the oxida tion pond discharges, and then  in the next year the 
classification was changed back again. There was an early claim to the Waitangi 
Tribunal and a whole series of appeals. The Act, which this bill repeals, cut across those 
local tensions and challenges and it gave  the Mount Maunganui Borough Council the 
authority to proceed with this destructiv e reclamation and to construct the ponds. 
Although we now have wetlands th at filter the discharge befo re it goes into the ocean, 
the way in which the land was taken remains enormously hurtful to Ng ā Pōtiki and, 
because of the hurt, to their ancestral landscap e. This bill is a small step in settling the 
claim and recognising the hurt that was caused.  
Just as that principal Act cut across th e local challenges to the Mount Maunganui 
Borough Council’s proposed scheme, today we  hear that the Minister for Primary 
Industries and this Government intend to change the Resource Management Act to 
make it much more difficult for those councils,  which are belatedly trying to deal with 
the impacts on our rivers, aquifers, and lakes, of the heavy nutrient burden that intensive 
agriculture is putting on these waterways.  Changing the Resource Management Act to 
impose a more onerous cost-ben efit test on councils when they are considering policies 
and rules to control the impacts of agricu ltural intensification would be creating an 
obstacle to the protection of our  rivers and lakes, just in the same way that the principal 
Act created the enormous hurt on this ance stral landscape by gi ving the council the 
authority to do this reclamation. Just as in this bill we are recognising the much greater 
value that we put on our estu aries and inshore coasts now, we need to better value our 
roto and our awa, and we need to remove that pollution burden that is happening now—
not because of human sewage so much, but more because of animal effluent.  
This bill is a step forward. I acknowle dge the Tauranga City Council and the 
partnership that it is developing with Ng ā Pōtiki. Certainly, at the Local Government 
and Environment Committee the joint submission from Ng ā Pōtiki and the city council 
wanted this bill to repeal the Act in a timely manner, and I think the House is doing that. 
We are very pleased as the Green Party to support the bill.

Can I just say that one of the features of this particular bill has been the speeches that

that evokes a lot of good feelings from peopl e, because it is unique. The story that goes 
with it is quite touching in many ways.  
Riccarton Bush is a small remnant of the podocarp forest that used to cover most of 
the Canterbury Plains. It exists because one of  the first families to settle in Canterbury, 
post-European times, were the two Deans brothers James and John Deans. They came to 
Canterbury, having previously been in the Wairarapa, to look for some land that was 
suitable for a sheep farming operation. Sadly, James Deans died in a drowning accident, 
trying to move some sheep to shore, fair ly soon after the brot hers had come to 
Canterbury. John laboured on for about a nother 10 years, I think, setting up the 
property, before he returned to his native Scotland to marry his fiancée, whom we know 
as Jane Deans but who was Jane McIlraith. They then came back to New Zealand. He 
caught what is described as a chill while crossing the isthmus of Panama, and died 
within about 6 months of them arriving b ack at Riccarton. So it  was really Jane 
Deans—Jane McIlraith—who did such a splend id job in developing that estate over a 
period of time, and then her son, John Deans II, after her.  
The other point that is useful to note in this  is that the Deans br others became fairly 
fluent in Te Reo Māori, and the lease they had is to this day recognised by Ngāi Tahu as 
being a very genuine document. It gave them a leasehold over a radius of 6 miles from 
the site of Riccarton House today. It was wh en the European settlement was begun in a 
big way in 1850 that the property began to be split up, and they eventually took up some 
holdings in the Malvern Hills. The contributio n of that family to Canterbury has been 
enormous, and it will continue to be so.  
The trust today is chaired by Charles Deans,  a descendant of the family. The real 
gem that is there is not the splendid house, which has survived the earthquakes, nor is it 
the first house, which was built on the Canterbury Plains, nor the oaks that were planted 
from seed provided by Governor George Gr ey, but, in fact, the perhaps 1,000-year-old 
or 1,500-year-old bush that grows there toda y, just as it once did across most of the 
Canterbury Plains.  
This piece of legislation updates several prev ious Acts of Parliament that have seen 
the trust survive since 1914, when the Deans family first gifted the bush to the city; 
from 1947, when the property was sold at a ve ry reasonable rate—that is, the remaining 
property—to the city; and then, of cour se, through the amalgamation period of 1989, 
when it was put inside Christchurch City but remained as a separate trust entity. This 
bill protects that. The Christchurch City Council has done a great deal of work in 
ensuring that that does happen. My associatio n was as a trustee and then chair of the 
trust for quite some years. We had a good relationship with the Christchurch City 
Council, which saw proposals to turn the very historic home there into a sort of wine bar 
and nightclub, instead of the wonderful restored  home that it is toda y. It is a piece of 
Canterbury’s history, a piece of Canterbury’s heritage, and ve ry well protected because 
of the work of the trust. So I wish the trus t well in the future, commend this bill to the 
House, thank all MPs who have taken such an  interest in it, and look forward to its 
passage very shortly.
